name: Formation of the Earth
summary: The Earth formed approximately 4.54 billion years ago by accretion of material from the solar nebula.
body:
Earth formed about **4.54 billion years ago** out of the disc of dust and gas left over from the Sun's formation. Successively larger fragments of that material collided and stuck together until a planet-sized body had assembled, most of it within about 10 to 20 million years. The heat released left the surface molten, and the planet sorted itself into a metallic core and a rocky mantle.

Iron and other heavy metals sank towards the centre in an episode sometimes called the iron catastrophe, within roughly ten million years of the start of accretion; lighter silicates rose to form the mantle and the earliest crust. Core formation gave the planet a magnetic field. That first crust was repeatedly destroyed and remade, and no rock of it survives anywhere.

The age is established by radiometric dating rather than by any surviving terrestrial rock. Meteorites that never melted preserve the age of the solar system's first solids, about 4.567 billion years; the oldest terrestrial material of any kind is detrital zircon from Western Australia at about 4.4 billion years. The conventional figure for Earth itself carries an uncertainty of around one per cent.

Within the first hundred million years a Mars-sized body struck the growing planet, and the debris became [the Moon](event:theia-impact). Gases released from the interior, together with water most likely delivered by asteroidal material, condensed into [the first oceans](event:first-oceans). The Hadean eon, which covers this whole interval, ended about 4 billion years ago.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Earth).

name: Giant impact forms the Moon
summary: A Mars-sized body, Theia, collided with the proto-Earth; debris from the impact coalesced into the Moon.
body:
The giant-impact hypothesis is the standard explanation for the Moon's origin. A protoplanet about the size of Mars, named Theia, struck [the proto-Earth](event:earth-formation) roughly 4.5 billion years ago, between about 20 and 100 million years after the solar system formed, with several recent estimates clustering nearer 4.45 billion. Material vaporised and thrown into orbit by the collision re-accumulated as the Moon.

Three lines of evidence support it. The Earth–Moon system carries an anomalously high angular momentum, which a glancing impact would supply. The Moon has only a small iron core, as expected if it formed largely from mantle material while Theia's core sank into Earth. And lunar and terrestrial rocks have stable-isotope ratios identical to within measurement error, which points to a common origin.

That last point is also the hypothesis's main difficulty. A simple impact model predicts that the Moon should be built mostly from the impactor and should therefore differ isotopically from Earth. Models that mix the two bodies more thoroughly, or that begin with a faster-spinning proto-Earth, are attempts to resolve it; the abundance of water and of volatile elements in lunar basalts is a further open question.

The aftermath left Earth spinning with a day of about five hours, which tides have since slowed, and the Moon much closer than it is now. The Moon's pull has kept Earth's axial tilt from wandering as widely as it otherwise would.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant-impact_hypothesis).

name: First oceans
summary: Liquid water condensed on Earth's surface as the crust cooled.
body:
Liquid water was present at Earth's surface very early, by about 4.4 billion years ago, within roughly 150 million years of [the planet's formation](event:earth-formation). The evidence is indirect, because no rock of that age survives; what remains are individual crystals eroded out of rock that is itself long gone.

Detrital zircons from the Jack Hills of Western Australia have been dated to 4.404 ± 0.008 billion years, and their oxygen-isotope ratios indicate that the magma they crystallised from had interacted with water at or near the surface. Pillow basalts from the Isua belt in Greenland, which form only under water, show unambiguously that oceans existed by 3.8 billion years ago.

Where the water came from is still argued. Earth may have accreted water-bearing material directly, since its building blocks were not all dry; it may have been delivered later by asteroids in a late veneer; or it may have arrived with the body that formed the Moon. The deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio of seawater matches carbonaceous asteroids far better than it matches most comets, which is the main reason asteroids are now favoured over comets as the principal source.

Once oceans existed they never wholly disappeared, and they are the setting in which [life](event:abiogenesis) appears not long afterwards.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origin_of_water_on_Earth).

name: Late Heavy Bombardment
summary: A hypothesised spike in asteroid and comet impacts on the inner Solar System, inferred from the ages of lunar impact melts; the evidence is disputed.
body:
The Late Heavy Bombardment is a hypothesised interval, roughly 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago, during which the Moon and the other inner planets were struck far more often than before or since. It was proposed after the Apollo missions returned impact-melt rocks whose ages clustered in a narrow band near 3.9 billion years.

The leading explanation is the Nice model, in which a late rearrangement of the giant planets' orbits scattered small bodies from the outer solar system and the asteroid belt inward. On that account the Moon's great impact basins (Imbrium, Serenitatis, Nectaris) all date from one episode.

The hypothesis is contested. Most Apollo samples come from a small area of the near side, and the clustering of ages may record ejecta from a single basin, Imbrium, rather than a solar-system-wide event. The absence of older impact melts may mean that they were destroyed rather than that earlier impacts did not occur. Later work on lunar and asteroidal meteorites has not settled the question, and definitive evidence is still lacking.

Earth, being larger, would have received far more impacts than the Moon, but plate tectonics and erosion have erased every crater of that age, so nothing on Earth tests the idea directly. [The oldest continental crust](event:earliest-continents) and the first chemical traces of [life](event:abiogenesis) both date from around the end of the proposed interval.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Heavy_Bombardment).

name: Origin of life
summary: Self-replicating chemical systems emerged, likely around hydrothermal vents, forming the first cellular life.
body:
Abiogenesis is the natural process by which living systems arose from non-living chemistry. It is understood not as a single event but as a sequence of steps of increasing complexity: the synthesis of organic molecules, the appearance of self-replicating polymers, and the enclosure of that chemistry within a membrane. The geological record places the transition between roughly 4.3 and 3.5 billion years ago.

The earliest claimed physical evidence, putative microbialites in the Nuvvuagittuq greenstone belt of Quebec, possibly 4.28 billion years old, is disputed. Biogenic graphite in 3.7-billion-year-old metasedimentary rocks from Greenland, identified by its depleted carbon-13 content, is more widely accepted, and the 3.48-billion-year-old [stromatolites](event:stromatolites) of the Dresser Formation in Western Australia are the oldest structures most researchers accept as built by life.

Several hypotheses compete over the setting and the chemistry. The RNA world proposes an early phase in which RNA both carried information and catalysed reactions, before DNA and proteins divided those roles between them. Submarine alkaline hydrothermal vents are a favoured environment because they maintain a continuous chemical disequilibrium between hydrogen-rich fluid and carbon dioxide dissolved in seawater. The Miller–Urey experiment of 1952 showed that amino acids form spontaneously from simple gases under prebiotic conditions, though the strongly reducing atmosphere it assumed is no longer thought to be the right one.

Every organism alive descends from a single ancestral population, the last universal common ancestor. Reconstructions from genes shared across the tree of life describe it as already complex: anaerobic, dependent on the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway for fixing carbon, and living in a hydrothermal setting. It was not the first life, only the one lineage whose descendants survive.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abiogenesis).

name: Formation of earliest continental crust
summary: Light crustal material accumulated into protocontinents, the first permanent continental landmasses.
body:
Earth's earliest crust was destroyed about as fast as it formed. By roughly 3.8 billion years ago, patches of thick, silica-rich crust had become buoyant enough to resist being recycled into the mantle. These are the cratons: the ancient, stable cores around which every modern continent has since been assembled.

A craton has two parts. The shield is the crystalline basement where it reaches the surface, as in Canada, Scandinavia, Western Australia and southern Africa; the platform is the same basement buried under younger sedimentary cover. What keeps a craton intact is its root, a keel of mantle extending several hundred kilometres down, depleted in iron and unusually dry, and so buoyant and stiff enough to ride above the convecting mantle for billions of years.

Most cratonisation happened during the Archean, between about 4 and 2.5 billion years ago, with further additions through the Proterozoic. The oldest intact rock yet dated, the Acasta Gneiss of north-western Canada, is about 4.03 billion years old.

Continental crust is the raw material of every later supercontinent, including [Rodinia](event:rodinia) and [Pangaea](event:pangaea), and its weathering is one of the principal long-term controls on atmospheric carbon dioxide.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craton).

name: Earliest stromatolites
summary: Layered microbial structures in Western Australia provide some of the earliest direct evidence of life.
body:
Part of [Origin of life](event:abiogenesis). Stromatolites are layered sedimentary structures built by communities of microbes, and they are among the oldest direct evidence of life on Earth. The Dresser and Strelley Pool formations of the Pilbara craton in Western Australia contain examples dated to about 3.48 billion years ago.

They form where a microbial mat (usually dominated by cyanobacteria) traps and binds sediment with the sticky polysaccharides it secretes, and where carbonate precipitates between the grains. The mat grows upward to stay in the light, and the result is a domed or columnar rock of fine laminations, each one a former mat surface.

Telling a stromatolite built by microbes from a similar shape precipitated chemically is a persistent difficulty, and the biological origin of the oldest examples has been argued over for decades. Supporting evidence includes clusters of organic globules and particular carbonate microtextures preserved within the laminae.

Stromatolites were a major component of shallow marine environments through the Precambrian and were at their most abundant about 1.25 billion years ago, after which they declined, probably because grazing and burrowing animals began to destroy the mats. Living examples survive where the water is too saline for grazers, notably at Hamelin Pool in Shark Bay, Western Australia.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stromatolite).

name: Anoxygenic photosynthesis
summary: Purple and green bacteria evolved photosynthetic pathways that used hydrogen sulphide and dissolved iron as electron donors rather than water.
body:
Anoxygenic photosynthesis captures light energy without splitting water and without releasing oxygen. It is used by several groups of bacteria (purple bacteria, green sulphur bacteria, heliobacteria and filamentous phototrophs among them), and it evolved before the oxygen-producing kind.

Instead of water, these organisms take electrons from hydrogen sulphide, molecular hydrogen or dissolved ferrous iron, all of which give up electrons more readily than water does. The waste products are elemental sulphur or oxidised iron rather than oxygen, and only a single photosystem is required. Archean sediments, in which ferric iron minerals are scarce, are consistent with photosynthesis of this kind operating long before free oxygen was being made anywhere.

The pathway was the dominant form of photosynthesis for hundreds of millions of years, and it remains widespread: in anoxic sediments, in stratified lakes, in hot springs, around hydrothermal vents and in the lower layers of microbial mats, wherever light penetrates but oxygen does not.

Its successor, [oxygenic photosynthesis](event:oxygenic-photosynthesis), uses water, which is effectively unlimited. That is why it displaced anoxygenic pathways from sunlit surface waters and went on to change the composition of the atmosphere.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anoxygenic_photosynthesis).

name: Peak of banded iron formations
summary: Iron oxides and silica were deposited in layers as oxygen from biological sources reacted with dissolved iron in the oceans.
body:
Banded iron formations are sedimentary rocks made of alternating layers of iron oxide and iron-poor chert or shale. Individual formations can be hundreds of metres thick and traceable for hundreds of kilometres. Nearly all are Precambrian: most accumulated in the late Archean, between about 2.8 and 2.5 billion years ago, with a second concentration around 1.85 billion years ago.

They are read as a record of the oxygenation of the oceans. The early sea held large quantities of dissolved ferrous iron, which stays in solution only where there is no oxygen. Oxygen released by [cyanobacteria](event:oxygenic-photosynthesis) converted it to insoluble ferric iron, which precipitated to the sea floor. The banding records a cycling between iron-rich and silica-rich deposition (annual or tidal rather than daily), though the mechanism behind it is still argued.

A small number of much younger formations, around 750 million years old, are associated with the glacial deposits of [Snowball Earth](event:snowball-earth), when an ocean sealed beneath ice would again have gone anoxic.

They are the world's principal source of iron ore, holding more than sixty per cent of global reserves, and are mined in Australia, Brazil, Canada, India, Russia, South Africa, Ukraine and the United States.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banded_iron_formation).

name: Oxygenic photosynthesis evolves
summary: Cyanobacteria evolved the ability to split water molecules using light energy, producing free oxygen as a byproduct.
body:
Cyanobacteria evolved a form of photosynthesis that splits water to obtain electrons and releases oxygen as waste. The oxygen it released changed the composition of Earth's atmosphere, and every plant and alga performs it today using chloroplasts descended from cyanobacteria taken up as endosymbionts.

Splitting water demands a far stronger oxidant than earlier [anoxygenic pathways](event:anoxygenic-photosynthesis) needed. It is achieved by linking two photosystems in series and by a manganese cluster that strips electrons from water molecules four at a time. What it buys is an inexhaustible electron donor: unlike hydrogen sulphide or dissolved iron, water is everywhere.

When this happened is not settled. Geological evidence puts oxygenic photosynthesis in place by at least 2.45 to 2.32 billion years ago; arguments from biomarkers and molecular clocks for cyanobacteria at 2.7 or even 3.5 billion years are contested. Atmospheric oxygen nonetheless stayed at or below about a thousandth of a per cent of today's level until 2.4 billion years ago, because the oxygen produced was consumed as fast as it was made, by dissolved iron, by volcanic gases and by reduced minerals at the surface.

Once those sinks were exhausted, oxygen accumulated: the [Great Oxidation Event](event:great-oxidation).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria).

name: Great Oxidation Event
summary: Free oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere for the first time, proving toxic to most existing life and oxidising iron across the planet's surface.
body:
The Great Oxidation Event was the first accumulation of free oxygen in Earth's atmosphere and shallow seas, beginning about 2.46 to 2.43 billion years ago. Oxygen made by [cyanobacteria](event:oxygenic-photosynthesis) had been consumed for hundreds of millions of years by dissolved iron, volcanic gases and reduced minerals; once those sinks could no longer keep up, it began to build up in the air.

Oxygen destroyed atmospheric methane, a far stronger greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, and the loss of that warming is the standard explanation for [the Huronian glaciation](event:huronian-glaciation). It was lethal to most of the anaerobic life then existing, and one estimate puts the resulting reduction of the biosphere at around eighty per cent. It also made aerobic respiration possible, which extracts far more energy per unit of food than fermentation, and it built an ozone layer. By reacting with rock at the surface it more than doubled the number of mineral species on Earth, adding some 2,500 varieties.

Oxygen did not simply rise and stay. It overshot in the middle of the event and then fell back, and the atmosphere held only around a tenth of its modern oxygen content by the end. It stayed near that level for more than a billion years afterwards, until the [Neoproterozoic oxygenation](event:tonian-oxygenation). The phases are set out in the steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Oxidation_Event).

steps.name: Oxygen begins to accumulate
steps.page:
Sulphur isotopes in sedimentary rocks record the disappearance of mass-independent fractionation, a signature that can only be produced when the atmosphere is essentially free of oxygen and ultraviolet light reaches sulphur dioxide unshielded. Its loss, between about 2.46 and 2.43 billion years ago, is the sharpest marker of the transition, and it is what dates the event.

Oxygen levels at this stage were still tiny by modern standards, but enough to change how iron, sulphur and manganese behaved at the Earth's surface, and enough to begin destroying atmospheric methane.

steps.name: Lomagundi–Jatuli excursion
steps.page:
The largest and longest positive carbon-isotope excursion in the geological record, registered in carbonate rocks on several continents. A carbonate signature this heavy implies that organic carbon was being buried on an enormous scale, and burying organic carbon is what leaves oxygen behind. Estimates of atmospheric oxygen during the excursion run as high as modern levels.

It is the high-water mark of the event rather than its steady state: the excursion ends, and the isotopic record swings back.

steps.name: Return to low oxygen
steps.page:
The Lomagundi excursion is followed by a sharp reversal associated with the deposition of vast volumes of organic-rich black shale, known as the Shunga–Francevillian event. Oxygen production could not be sustained at the earlier rate once the nutrients supporting it had been drawn down, and atmospheric oxygen fell back to a low level.

It stayed there for most of the next billion and a half years, an interval sometimes called the boring billion, until the [Tonian oxygenation](event:tonian-oxygenation) began to raise it again.

name: Huronian glaciation
summary: The first documented global glaciation occurred when rising atmospheric oxygen destroyed methane, reducing greenhouse warming.
body:
Part of [Great Oxidation Event](event:great-oxidation). The Huronian glaciation was a long series of ice ages between about 2.4 and 2.1 billion years ago, the earliest for which there is good evidence. It is named for glacial deposits north of Lake Huron in Ontario, and equivalent rocks are known from Michigan, Wyoming, Nunavut, South Africa, India and Australia.

Three distinct glacial episodes are recorded in the Ontario sequence, preserved in the Ramsay Lake, Bruce and Gowganda formations. The standard explanation ties them to the rise of oxygen: methane was a major greenhouse gas in the earlier atmosphere, and oxygen destroys it, converting it to the much weaker carbon dioxide and water vapour. The Sun was also fainter than it is today, and heat flow from the planet's interior was in decline.

Whether Earth froze over entirely, as the later [Cryogenian glaciations](event:snowball-earth) may have done, is not established. Palaeomagnetic evidence for ice at low latitudes is disputed, and glacial deposits interbedded with carbonates suggest temperate intervals between the advances.

Spanning some 300 million years, it is among the longest glacial epochs in Earth's history.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huronian_glaciation).

name: First eukaryotic cells
summary: A cell engulfed another cell, retaining it as an internal organelle; this established the compartmented eukaryotic cell with mitochondria.
body:
Eukaryotes are organisms whose cells keep their DNA inside a membrane-bound nucleus. Every animal, plant, fungus and alga is one, along with a great many single-celled organisms. The lineage arose when an archaeon took up a bacterium and kept it: that bacterium became the mitochondrion, and the merger is the defining event of eukaryogenesis.

Genomic work places the host among the Asgard archaea and the endosymbiont among the alphaproteobacteria. A second, later merger, this time with a cyanobacterium, produced chloroplasts, and with them the whole photosynthetic side of the eukaryotes, the algae and eventually the land plants. Both organelles still carry small genomes of their own and divide independently of the cell around them.

Dating the origin is difficult. Fossils that can be assigned confidently to living eukaryotic groups appear about 1.2 billion years ago, with red algae among the earliest. Older candidates exist, such as organic-walled microfossils from the Ruyang Group in China, 1.8 to 1.6 billion years old, but their affinities are uncertain, and molecular clocks generally give older dates than the fossils do.

The last eukaryotic common ancestor was a population rather than an individual, and it already had a nucleus, a flagellum, aerobic mitochondria and the machinery of [sexual reproduction](event:sexual-reproduction). What compartmentalisation and mitochondria bought was energy available per gene, which is the usual explanation for why this lineage alone produced large, complex [multicellular](event:multicellular-eukaryotes) bodies.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eukaryote).

name: Acritarchs and earliest eukaryotic fossils
summary: Microfossils with multiple wall layers indicate that eukaryotic life was diversifying before the emergence of animals and plants.
body:
Part of [First eukaryotic cells](event:eukaryotes). Acritarchs are small organic-walled microfossils whose biological affinities cannot be established with confidence. The name is a deliberate catch-all: it groups fossils by preservation and shape rather than by relationship, and different acritarchs almost certainly come from unrelated organisms.

Most are thought to be the resting cysts of single-celled marine algae, comparable to those made by living dinoflagellates. They are built of a tough, decay-resistant organic material and are recovered by dissolving the surrounding rock in hydrofluoric acid. The earliest specimens confidently identified as eukaryotic come from rocks between about 2.15 and 1.95 billion years old; older Archean examples may well be prokaryotic.

Because they are abundant, widespread and quick to change, acritarchs are valuable index fossils for dating Palaeozoic marine rocks where nothing else is available, and for reconstructing ancient marine environments.

Their record also tracks the fortunes of the plankton. Diversity and size increased sharply around a billion years ago, with the appearance of elaborate spines usually read as defences against predators; the [Cryogenian glaciations](event:snowball-earth) cut diversity heavily; the group flourished again through the [Cambrian](event:cambrian-explosion) and the rest of the Palaeozoic, and collapsed at the end of the Permian.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acritarch).

name: First multicellular eukaryotes
summary: Eukaryotic cells formed multicellular colonies with specialised functions, establishing multicellular life.
body:
Multicellularity (cells staying together and dividing labour rather than dispersing) evolved independently many times over. Estimates run to at least twenty-five separate origins among eukaryotes and several among bacteria. Complex multicellularity, with genuinely differentiated tissues, arose in only six eukaryotic groups: animals, fungi, land plants, and the green, red and brown algae.

The earliest widely accepted eukaryotic example is *Bangiomorpha pubescens*, a filamentous red alga from Arctic Canada about 1.05 billion years old, which shows differentiated cells and a holdfast for anchoring to the sea floor. Older candidates are contested: the centimetre-scale coiled fossil *Grypania* and the Francevillian structures from Gabon, both Palaeoproterozoic, may or may not be eukaryotic or even biological. Decimetre-scale multicellular fossils are known from about 1.56 billion years ago in China.

Explanations for the transition include cells failing to separate after division and then specialising, aggregation of separate cells into a colony, and defence against single-celled predators, which cannot swallow a clump. Rising oxygen is a common permissive factor in these accounts, since a larger body needs more of it to diffuse inward.

Complex multicellular life became abundant only much later, after the [Cryogenian glaciations](event:snowball-earth), with the [Ediacaran biota](event:ediacaran) and then the [Cambrian explosion](event:cambrian-explosion).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multicellular_organism).

name: Evolution of sexual reproduction
summary: Eukaryotes evolved meiosis and cellular fusion, allowing genetic recombination and accelerated adaptation to environmental change.
body:
Sexual reproduction combines meiosis, which halves the number of chromosomes, with the fusion of two gametes, which restores it. Offspring therefore carry a reshuffled mixture of two parents' genes rather than a copy of one. It is an ancestral eukaryotic trait: the last common ancestor of all [eukaryotes](event:eukaryotes) already had it.

Estimates for its origin range from about two billion years ago to about 1.2 billion. The oldest fossil usually cited as direct evidence is *Bangiomorpha pubescens*, a red alga from Arctic Canada roughly 1.05 billion years old, which preserves differentiated spores and so implies a sexual life cycle.

Why sex persists is a long-standing problem, because it is expensive. An asexual population of the same size produces twice as many offspring per generation, since males bear none, the two-fold cost of sex. The main proposed compensations are that recombination during meiosis repairs double-strand breaks in DNA and masks harmful recessive mutations; that reshuffling genes lets a host stay ahead of faster-breeding parasites, the Red Queen argument; and that recombination can undo the irreversible accumulation of deleterious mutations that afflicts asexual lineages, known as Muller's ratchet.

Whatever the balance among those, recombination gave eukaryotes a faster route to variation than mutation alone, and it is the genetic setting for the later evolution of [multicellular bodies](event:multicellular-eukaryotes).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolution_of_sexual_reproduction).

name: Rodinia supercontinent
summary: Nearly all continental crust consolidated into a single supercontinent before subsequent rifting and dispersal.
body:
Rodinia was a supercontinent that assembled most of the world's continental crust between about 1.26 and 0.90 billion years ago and broke apart between roughly 750 and 633 million years ago. It was surrounded by a single superocean, Mirovia.

Its existence is inferred from matching belts of deformed rock on continents now far apart, chiefly the Grenville orogeny of eastern North America and its equivalents in Scandinavia, South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica. The arrangement of the core cratons is reasonably well established; the positions of Siberia and the Chinese blocks relative to Laurentia are not, and several competing reconstructions are in use.

Rifting created long stretches of new continental margin at low latitudes, flooded continental interiors with shallow seas, and exposed fresh basalt to tropical rainfall. Silicate weathering consumes carbon dioxide, so a great deal of new rock weathering in the wet tropics is one of the standard explanations for the extreme cooling that followed, the [Cryogenian glaciations](event:snowball-earth) between 717 and 635 million years ago, and indirectly for the conditions in which large multicellular life appeared.

Continental crust gathered again into [Pangaea](event:pangaea) some 400 million years later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodinia).

name: Tonian oxygenation and radiation
summary: Atmospheric oxygen levels increased episodically during this period while eukaryotic life diversified.
body:
The Tonian, from 1,000 to 720 million years ago, is the first period of the Neoproterozoic. It is the interval in which [Rodinia](event:rodinia) began to come apart, atmospheric oxygen rose again after more than a billion years at a low level, and eukaryotic life diversified in ways visible in the fossil record.

At least two distinct oxygenation episodes are recorded in the Tonian, part of the longer Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event. Carbon-isotope values in marine carbonates rise substantially in the later part of the period, which implies large-scale burial of organic carbon and therefore a net release of oxygen. Higher oxygen made possible the energy-hungry metabolic pathways characteristic of later animal life.

The biological changes run alongside. [Acritarchs](event:acritarchs) underwent their first large radiation. Fossils interpreted as sponges have been reported from rocks 890 to 800 million years old, and structures resembling fungal mycelium from 810 to 715 million years ago. Early seaweeds appear, while [stromatolites](event:stromatolites), which had dominated shallow marine environments for two billion years, begin their long decline.

The period ends with the onset of the [Cryogenian glaciations](event:snowball-earth).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonian).

name: Snowball Earth
summary: Glaciers advanced toward the equator, possibly covering the entire ocean surface, during the Cryogenian period.
body:
Snowball Earth is the hypothesis that the planet froze from the poles almost or entirely to the equator during the Cryogenian period, between about 717 and 635 million years ago. Two glaciations are involved: the Sturtian, roughly 717 to 660 million years ago, and the Marinoan, roughly 650 to 635. Each lasted for tens of millions of years, far longer than any later ice age.

The evidence is geological. Glacial deposits of this age are found on nearly every continent, and palaeomagnetic measurements place some of them (in Svalbard, Greenland and Australia) at tropical latitudes at the time. Dropstones released from floating ice sit embedded in marine sediments. Above the glacial rocks lie distinctive layers of carbonate, tens of metres thick and deposited very rapidly; these cap carbonates are read as the product of intense chemical weathering under a carbon-dioxide-rich atmosphere immediately after the ice melted. [Banded iron formations](event:banded-iron-formations-peak) briefly reappear, which requires an ocean that had gone anoxic beneath a lid of ice.

The usual account of how it began involves large volcanic provinces erupting in the wet tropics as [Rodinia](event:rodinia) broke apart: weathering the fresh basalt drew down carbon dioxide, cooling produced ice, and ice reflected sunlight, cooling the planet further. Ending it required volcanic carbon dioxide to accumulate for millions of years beneath the ice until the greenhouse effect overwhelmed the albedo, after which deglaciation would have been very fast.

A weaker version, the slushball, keeps a belt of open or thin ice around the equator. Some sedimentary structures indicate moving ice and open water, and climate models have difficulty freezing the whole ocean without altering other assumptions. Either way the episodes end immediately before the appearance of the [Ediacaran biota](event:ediacaran) and, a little later, the [Cambrian explosion](event:cambrian-explosion).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowball_Earth).

name: Ediacaran biota
summary: The first large soft-bodied multicellular organisms appeared in the fossil record.
body:
The Ediacaran biota were the first large, complex multicellular organisms. Most were soft-bodied and fixed in place, and their relationship to living groups is uncertain. They are named after the Ediacara Hills of South Australia, where they were first recognised, and they have been found on every continent except Antarctica.

Three successive assemblages are distinguished. The Avalon assemblage, about 575 to 565 million years ago and known best from Newfoundland and from Charnwood Forest in England, is dominated by deep-water rangeomorphs such as *Charnia*, built on a repeating fractal branching plan. The White Sea assemblage, 560 to 550 million years ago in Russia and Australia, is the most diverse and includes *Dickinsonia* and *Kimberella*. The Nama assemblage, 550 to 539 million years ago in Namibia, shows high turnover and preserves the first animals with mineralised skeletons.

What these organisms were is still argued. They have been interpreted as animals, as algae, as lichens or fungi, as giant protists, and as an extinct grade of their own, the Vendobionta. Sterol biomarkers extracted from *Dickinsonia* in 2018 support an animal affinity for at least that genus, and *Kimberella* is associated with scratch marks that look like grazing traces.

Almost all of them disappear at the base of the Cambrian, 538.8 million years ago. The microbial mats they lived on disappear at the same time, and one explanation is that burrowing and grazing animals of the [Cambrian explosion](event:cambrian-explosion) destroyed the substrate the community depended on.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ediacaran_biota).

name: Cambrian explosion
summary: Nearly all modern animal body plans appeared in the fossil record within a period of tens of millions of years.
body:
The Cambrian explosion was an interval beginning about 538.8 million years ago during which most major animal groups appear in the fossil record for the first time. Within roughly 13 to 25 million years, animals with hard parts, jointed limbs, eyes and predatory habits are present in marine sediments worldwide, where before there had been little but microbes, algae and the soft-bodied [Ediacaran biota](event:ediacaran).

Three deposits of exceptional preservation carry most of what is known. The Chengjiang fauna of Yunnan and Sirius Passet in northern Greenland are early Cambrian; the [Burgess Shale](event:burgess-shale-fauna) of British Columbia is about 508 million years old. All three preserve soft tissue, which ordinary fossilisation destroys, and so record animals that would otherwise be invisible.

No single cause is agreed. Rising oxygen would have permitted larger and more active bodies. The appearance of predation could have set off an arms race between armour and the means of breaking it, though predators existed before the Cambrian. Changes in the developmental genes that govern body plans, particularly the Hox genes, allow large morphological changes to follow from small genetic ones. Higher calcium concentrations in seawater would have made mineralised skeletons cheaper to build.

How sudden it really was is also disputed. Molecular clocks put the divergence of the major animal lineages well back into the Neoproterozoic, and trace fossils show bilaterian animals moving through sediment before the Cambrian. Some researchers argue that the radiation was no faster than others in animal history, and that its apparent abruptness owes much to the sudden preservability of skeletons and to the incompleteness of the earlier record.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambrian_explosion).

name: Trilobite diversification and radiation
summary: Armoured arthropods with complex eyes and jointed limbs diversified throughout the oceans.
body:
Part of [Cambrian explosion](event:cambrian-explosion). Trilobites were marine arthropods with a three-lobed, heavily mineralised exoskeleton. They appear about 521 million years ago, radiate through the Cambrian and Ordovician, and are among the most abundant fossils of the whole Palaeozoic: more than 22,000 species have been described.

The body has three parts (a head shield, a thorax of between two and 103 articulated segments, and a tail plate), and the shell is calcite reinforced with calcium phosphate in a lattice of chitin. Their eyes are unusual: the lenses are calcite crystals oriented so that they focus light, the only mineral eyes known, and some species carried thousands of them. Many could roll up for protection, and all of them moulted, which is why one animal can leave many fossils.

Diversity peaked in the late Cambrian and the Ordovician, which marks the high point of their range of form. The [end-Ordovician extinction](event:ordovician-extinction) removed several groups, but about three-quarters of the late Ordovician fauna survived into the Silurian, after which the group declined steadily through the Devonian. Only two genera were still alive at the end of the Permian, and neither survived [the extinction](event:permian-extinction) there.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trilobite).

name: Burgess Shale exceptional preservation
summary: Rapid sediment deposition buried soft-bodied animals, preserving anatomical details normally lost in fossil formation.
body:
Part of [Cambrian explosion](event:cambrian-explosion). The Burgess Shale, in Yoho National Park in the Canadian Rockies, preserves a middle Cambrian marine community about 508 million years old in exceptional detail, including animals with no mineralised parts at all. Charles Walcott found it on 30 August 1909 and collected some 65,000 specimens over the following two decades.

Preservation happened because animals were swept off a shallow carbonate platform and buried rapidly in fine mud at the foot of it, before decay could proceed far. Soft tissues survive as carbonaceous films less than a micrometre thick, including guts, gills, limbs, eyes, and in a few cases nervous tissue.

The fauna includes *Anomalocaris*, a large swimming predator; *Opabinia*, with five eyes and a grasping proboscis; *Hallucigenia*, which was reconstructed upside down for years; *Wiwaxia*, armoured with scales and spines; and *Pikaia*, a chordate.

Walcott assigned everything he found to living groups. Reinterpretation from the 1970s onward found many animals that fitted nowhere, and Stephen Jay Gould's *Wonderful Life* (1989) presented them as failed experiments in body plan and as evidence that the history of life was contingent. Simon Conway Morris argued in reply that nearly all of them can be placed within or close to modern phyla, and that reading is now the more common one. The site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgess_Shale).

name: Ordovician reef and coral ecosystems
summary: Shallow-water reef ecosystems constructed by corals, sponges, and bryozoans became prominent seafloor features.
body:
Reefs built by animals became a permanent feature of shallow seas during the Ordovician, 485 to 443 million years ago. Tabulate and rugose corals, stromatoporoid sponges and bryozoans replaced the microbial and archaeocyathid mounds of the Cambrian, and the kind of rigid framework they built has had counterparts in every period since.

The change was one part of a much larger event, the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, which ran from roughly 497 to 467 million years ago. The number of marine orders doubled and the number of families roughly tripled. Brachiopods, bryozoans, crinoids, gastropods, bivalves, cephalopods and graptolites all radiated; plankton and the animals feeding on it diversified in step; and [trilobites](event:trilobite-diversification) and cephalopods colonised open water. The result was a marine fauna dominated by attached suspension feeders, which persisted for the rest of the Palaeozoic.

Proposed drivers include rising oxygen, cooling seas, palaeogeographic and tectonic changes that created more shallow shelf, and increased nutrient delivery from mountain building. Reefs then supported further diversification in their own right, since a rigid framework creates a great many small habitats.

Much of it was undone at the end of the period by the [Ordovician–Silurian extinction](event:ordovician-extinction).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordovician).

name: Radiation of early fish and agnathans
summary: Jawless fish diversified in freshwater and marine environments, establishing vertebrates as a successful lineage.
body:
Vertebrates begin as small, jawless, filter-feeding animals. The earliest are Cambrian. *Myllokunmingia* and *Haikouichthys* from the Chengjiang deposits of Yunnan already have a notochord, segmented muscle blocks and gills. Conodonts, known mainly from their tooth-like elements, appear at about the same time and persist until the Triassic.

From the middle Ordovician onward, armoured jawless fish collectively called ostracoderms spread through marine and fresh water. *Arandaspis* from central Australia and *Sacabambaspis* from Bolivia are among the earliest with substantial bony armour. Groups such as the osteostracans and heterostracans carried heavy dermal head shields; the thelodonts had small mineralised scales instead. None had jaws or paired fins in the modern sense, and most lived on or near the bottom.

Bone, dentine and enamel, the tissues later vertebrates use for skeletons and teeth, appear first in this armour, which is why the origin of the vertebrate skeleton is bound up with these animals.

Jaws evolved in the early Silurian by modification of the foremost gill arches, and the [jawed fish](event:devonian-fish-revolution) that resulted took over during the Devonian. Jawless fish declined sharply and never recovered; only the hagfish and lampreys survive.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnatha).

name: Plants colonise the land
summary: Spore-bearing plants colonized terrestrial environments, beginning the development of continental vegetation.
body:
Plants moved onto land in the middle Ordovician, around 470 million years ago. The first evidence is not of plants themselves but of their spores: cryptospores with tough sporopollenin walls, recovered from Ordovician rocks in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere on Gondwana, comparable to those produced by living liverworts.

Land plants descend from freshwater green algae, from among the charophytes, the group modern stoneworts belong to. The move demanded solutions to desiccation, structural support and the transport of water, and these arrived over the following hundred million years rather than at once. Simple conducting cells appear in the Silurian; true vascular tissue with lignin-strengthened walls, which resists collapse under tension, follows, and *Cooksonia* from the later Silurian is the earliest known vascular plant. Roots developed gradually through the Devonian, from rhizoids a few millimetres deep to systems reaching nearly a metre. Broad leaves became common around 360 million years ago, once falling carbon dioxide made a large light-gathering surface worth its cost in water.

The consequences for the planet were large. Roots broke up rock and acidified soils, deepening chemical weathering and drawing down carbon dioxide; sediment began to be retained on land, and mudrock becomes markedly more common in the record from the Ordovician onward. [Animals followed the vegetation](event:silurian-land-colonisation) ashore, and by the Carboniferous plants had built [forests](event:carboniferous-forests) dense enough to bury carbon on a global scale.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionary_history_of_plants).

name: Ordovician–Silurian extinction
summary: Approximately 85% of marine species went extinct as glaciation locked up seawater and drained the shallow continental shelves.
body:
The Late Ordovician mass extinction, about 445 to 443 million years ago, was the first of the five largest extinctions in the fossil record and the second largest by proportion of genera lost. Between 49 and 60 per cent of marine genera and close to 85 per cent of marine species disappeared. Life was still almost entirely marine, so the event is recorded only in the sea.

It came in two pulses. The first, at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary, coincides with the rapid growth of an ice sheet over Gondwana, which then lay across the South Pole. The world shifted from greenhouse to icehouse within a geologically short time; sea level fell, draining the shallow continental shelves where most life lived, and water temperatures dropped faster than warm-adapted species could tolerate.

The second pulse came in the late Hirnantian as the glaciation ended. Rising sea level was accompanied by widespread anoxia and euxinia (oxygen-depleted, sulphidic water), which spread across the shelves and persisted into the early Silurian.

Brachiopods, bryozoans, [trilobites](event:trilobite-diversification), conodonts, echinoderms, corals and graptolites were all heavily affected, and the [reef ecosystems](event:ordovician-reef-ecosystems) of the period were dismantled. Unlike later extinctions it eliminated few whole groups: the fauna that recovered through the Silurian was much the same one, at lower diversity.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Ordovician_mass_extinction).

name: Silurian land colonisation by arthropods
summary: Millipedes and early arachnids colonized terrestrial environments, breathing air and hunting among primitive plants.
body:
Animals followed plants onto land during the Silurian, 443 to 419 million years ago. The colonists were arthropods (millipedes, centipedes and early arachnids), small and still dependent on damp ground, but breathing air.

*Pneumodesmus newmani*, from Stonehaven in Scotland, is the oldest animal known to have breathed air: its cuticle preserves spiracles, and it dates to about 425 million years ago. *Kampecaris obanensis* from Kerrera in the Inner Hebrides is a millipede of similar age. Trigonotarbids, extinct relatives of spiders, are known from around 420 million years ago in Britain, and comparable faunas come from Wales and Germany. Trackways and burrows extend the record a little further back.

These animals lived among the first vascular [land plants](event:land-plants), low, leafless, spore-bearing forms such as *Cooksonia*, rarely more than a few centimetres tall. The earliest terrestrial food webs seem to have been built on decaying plant matter and on predation: there is little evidence of anything eating living plant tissue at this stage, and the arachnids were hunters.

Vertebrates were still confined to the water, and would not follow for another forty million years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silurian).

name: Devonian fish diversification and radiation
summary: Diverse jawed fish with varied body forms dominated the oceans during the Age of Fishes.
body:
The Devonian, 419 to 359 million years ago, is called the Age of Fishes because every major group of fish either appeared or reached its greatest diversity during it. Jawed vertebrates, which had evolved in the Silurian, displaced the [jawless fish](event:early-fish) that preceded them.

Placoderms, jawed fish with articulated bony armour over the head and trunk, were the dominant group for much of the period, and included *Dunkleosteus*, a predator several metres long with shearing bony plates in place of teeth. Cartilaginous fish, ancestors of sharks and rays, diversified alongside them, as did the two great groups of bony fish: the ray-finned fish, which today account for most vertebrate species, and the lobe-finned fish, whose paired fins contain a single proximal bone and a jointed skeleton beyond it.

That last arrangement is the one that became a limb. Lobe-finned fish such as *Eusthenopteron* and *Tiktaalik* show progressively more weight-bearing fin skeletons, flatter heads and more mobile necks, and it is from within this group that the first [tetrapods](event:tetrapods) came.

The [Late Devonian extinctions](event:devonian-extinction) eliminated the placoderms entirely and finished the armoured jawless fish with them.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devonian).

name: Vertebrates walk on land
summary: Lobe-finned fish with weight-bearing limbs, exemplified by Tiktaalik, moved onto land.
body:
Tetrapods, four-limbed vertebrates including all amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, evolved from lobe-finned fish during the Devonian. Their origin is among the best-documented major transitions in the fossil record, though the sequence is less tidy than it once appeared.

The oldest evidence is a set of trackways at Zachełmie in Poland, made about 390 million years ago by an animal walking on limbs with digits. Fragmentary body fossils of *Elginerpeton* from Scotland and *Obruchevichthys* from Latvia follow at around 380 million years, though not everyone accepts them as tetrapods. Nearly complete skeletons appear late in the Devonian: *Acanthostega* and *Ichthyostega* from East Greenland, which had limbs with digits (eight of them on *Acanthostega*) but also internal gills and a tail fin.

*Tiktaalik roseae*, found on Ellesmere Island in the Canadian Arctic in 2004 and about 375 million years old, is a lobe-finned fish rather than a tetrapod: a flattened skull, a neck, and fin skeletons robust enough to prop the body up. It postdates the Polish trackways, which is the main reason the transition is now thought to have begun earlier than the body fossils by themselves would suggest.

These animals were aquatic, and limbs appear to have evolved for moving through shallow, weed-choked water rather than for walking on land. Fully terrestrial tetrapods, with the [amniotic egg](event:amniotic-egg) to free them from standing water, are a Carboniferous development.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrapod).

name: Late Devonian extinction
summary: A series of extinction pulses over millions of years eliminated most reef ecosystems and shallow marine fauna.
body:
The Late Devonian extinction was not one event but a series of pulses spread over some fifteen million years at the end of the period. Two are severe enough to be named: the Kellwasser event, at the Frasnian–Famennian boundary about 372 million years ago, and the Hangenberg event, at the very end of the Devonian about 359 million years ago.

The losses were concentrated in shallow tropical seas. Around 40 per cent of marine species died in the Kellwasser event alone; across the whole interval perhaps 22 per cent of marine families, 57 per cent of genera and at least three-quarters of species failed to reach the Carboniferous. Reef builders were hit hardest. The stromatoporoid sponges and the tabulate and rugose corals nearly vanished, and reefs on that scale did not return for over a hundred million years. Placoderms were halved and then eliminated, and the armoured jawless fish went with them.

Both events are marked by black shale, the sediment of oxygen-starved water. The most-cited trigger is the spread of [land plants](event:land-plants): deep-rooting trees weathered rock, released nutrients into rivers and fertilised coastal seas into algal blooms that stripped the water of oxygen. The same weathering drew down carbon dioxide and cooled the climate. Volcanism from the Viluy province in Siberia has been proposed as a further cause.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Devonian_extinction).

name: Carboniferous coal forests
summary: Extensive swamp forests of lycopod trees accumulated large quantities of carbon that eventually became coal deposits.
body:
The coal forests were vast swamp and riverbank forests that covered much of the tropics during the later Carboniferous and the Permian. Their buried and compressed remains became most of the coal mined in Europe and eastern North America.

The dominant trees were lycopsids (*Lepidodendron* and *Sigillaria*), which grew to thirty metres or more on unbranched trunks supported by thick bark rather than by wood, alongside giant horsetails, tree ferns and early seed plants. Carbon accumulated because the equatorial belt of Euramerica lay over subsiding basins that stayed wet, so that dead plant matter piled up in waterlogged, acidic peat faster than it could rot. An older explanation, that fungi capable of breaking down lignin had not yet evolved, is now regarded as at most part of the answer.

Atmospheric oxygen rose to perhaps 25 to 30 per cent, against 21 per cent today, and the period is known for very large arthropods: the griffinfly *Meganeura*, with a wingspan of about 75 centimetres, and the millipede relative *Arthropleura*, up to 2.6 metres long.

The forests fragmented around 305 million years ago, in an episode called the Carboniferous rainforest collapse, as the climate began swinging between humid and arid. Tree ferns replaced the lycopsids, and drier conditions favoured the [amniotes](event:amniotic-egg) over the amphibians. The coal itself was dug up and burned 300 million years later, in the [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_forest).

name: Pangaea supercontinent
summary: Nearly all continental landmasses united into a single supercontinent surrounded by the Panthalassic Ocean.
body:
Pangaea was a supercontinent that assembled during the Carboniferous, around 335 million years ago, and began to break apart at the end of the Triassic, about 200 million years ago. It brought nearly all of the world's continental crust into one mass, surrounded by a single superocean, Panthalassa, with the Tethys opening into it from the east.

Its existence is why the same Permian and Triassic land fossils (*Glossopteris*, *Lystrosaurus*, *Mesosaurus*, *Cynognathus*) are found on continents now separated by oceans, an argument Alfred Wegener made in 1912 and which was accepted only after seafloor spreading was demonstrated in the 1960s. Matching mountain belts and rock sequences across the Atlantic point the same way.

A single landmass has little coastline for its area, and the interior of Pangaea was consequently very dry: one of the most extensive desert systems in Earth's history occupied it, with short rainy seasons even well inland. The loss of shallow continental shelf, where most marine life lives, is among the background stresses often invoked for the severity of the [end-Permian extinction](event:permian-extinction).

Breakup came in three phases. Rifting between North America and Africa began in the Triassic and had opened the central [Atlantic](event:atlantic-opening) by about 175 million years ago. Gondwana came apart from the Early Cretaceous, separating Africa, South America, India, Antarctica and Australia. Finally, in the early Cenozoic, Laurentia parted from Eurasia and the Norwegian Sea opened, 60 to 55 million years ago. The continents are still moving.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea).

name: Evolution of the amniotic egg
summary: The evolution of the amniotic egg permitted vertebrate reproduction independent of aquatic environments.
body:
Part of [Vertebrates walk on land](event:tetrapods). The amniotic egg encloses the embryo in a set of membranes that do, inside the shell, what a pond did for an amphibian embryo. The amnion holds fluid around the embryo, the chorion handles gas exchange, the allantois stores waste, and a large yolk supplies food. Together with internal fertilisation and a water-resistant skin, this is what freed vertebrate reproduction from standing water.

It also allowed the egg to grow larger and to exchange gas faster, so that a bigger and more active embryo could reach full development before hatching.

The oldest amniotes known from body fossils are *Hylonomus lyelli* and *Asaphestera*, small lizard-like animals about 318 million years old, found inside the hollow stumps of fossil trees at Joggins in Nova Scotia. *Casineria* from Scotland, around 340 million years old, lies close to the ancestry. Clawed footprints reported in 2025 from the Snowy Plains Formation in Australia, dated between 359 and 354 million years ago, would push the group's origin back into the Devonian.

Almost immediately after appearing, amniotes divided into two lineages that between them account for most large land vertebrates since: the synapsids, leading to [mammals](event:synapsid-domination), and the sauropsids, leading to reptiles, [dinosaurs](event:first-dinosaurs) and birds.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amniote).

name: Synapsid domination of Permian terrestrial ecosystems
summary: Synapsids, the amniote lineage leading to mammals, dominated terrestrial ecosystems as herbivores and predators.
body:
Synapsids are the branch of the [amniotes](event:amniotic-egg) that leads to mammals. They are distinguished by a single opening in the skull behind each eye socket, which gives the jaw muscles more room and a stronger bite. The earliest appear near the end of the Carboniferous, around 315 to 307 million years ago, and they were the largest land vertebrates of the Permian.

The early forms, informally called pelycosaurs, include *Dimetrodon*, a sprawling predator up to about four metres long with a tall skin-covered sail on its back, abundant in the red beds of Texas and Oklahoma. From one pelycosaur group came the therapsids, with more upright limbs, more differentiated teeth and probably higher metabolic rates. Therapsids dominated Permian land faunas as both herbivores (the barrel-bodied dicynodonts) and predators (the sabre-toothed gorgonopsians).

The [end-Permian extinction](event:permian-extinction) reduced them severely. Only the dicynodonts and a few carnivorous lines survived into the Triassic, where [archosaurs](event:first-dinosaurs) took over the large-bodied roles. One group of small, increasingly mammal-like cynodonts persisted through that displacement, and it is from these that the first [mammaliaforms](event:triassic-mammalian-radiation) emerged in the Late Triassic.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synapsida).

name: Permian–Triassic extinction
summary: Approximately 81% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrates went extinct in Earth's most severe biotic crisis.
body:
The Permian–Triassic extinction, about 252 million years ago, was the most severe biotic crisis in the fossil record, and is sometimes called the Great Dying. Around 81 per cent of marine species and some 70 per cent of terrestrial vertebrate species disappeared, along with 57 per cent of families and 62 per cent of genera. Precise dating of the boundary beds in South China places the main extinction between 251.941 and 251.880 million years ago, a window of roughly sixty thousand years.

The accepted cause is the eruption of the [Siberian Traps](event:siberian-traps), one of the largest volcanic events known. Magma intruded thick sequences of coal, carbonate and evaporite in the Tunguska basin and cooked them, so that the eruptions released far more carbon and halogen gas than the lava alone would have. Atmospheric carbon dioxide rose from roughly 400 to 2,500 parts per million and global temperature by around 8 °C. The oceans warmed, acidified and lost their oxygen; large areas became euxinic, charged with hydrogen sulphide. Ozone depletion and acid rain are also invoked.

Eight or nine orders of insects vanished, the only mass extinction that seriously affected them. [Trilobites](event:trilobite-diversification) ended here, as did the eurypterids and most of the range of form among crinoids, brachiopods and ammonoids. Around 93 per cent of foraminifera died. Reefs disappeared for millions of years. On land the [synapsids](event:synapsid-domination) that had dominated the Permian were reduced to a handful of surviving lines.

Recovery was slow and uneven. Some local marine communities were re-established within one or two million years and marine ecosystems were functioning again by the Middle Triassic, but terrestrial vertebrate faunas took around thirty million years to regain their complexity, and global marine diversity far longer. The depleted world of the Early Triassic is the one in which the [first dinosaurs](event:first-dinosaurs) appeared.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permian%E2%80%93Triassic_extinction_event).

name: Siberian Traps eruptions
summary: One of Earth's largest known volcanic events covered millions of square kilometres of Siberia with basalt.
body:
Part of [Permian–Triassic extinction](event:permian-extinction). The Siberian Traps are the remains of one of the largest volcanic events in Earth's history: a flood basalt province covering some seven million square kilometres of northern Eurasia, with an estimated volume of around four million cubic kilometres of igneous rock. Eruption spanned roughly two million years across the Permian–Triassic boundary, about 252 million years ago.

The rocks it erupted through also mattered. The Tunguska basin beneath it holds thick Palaeozoic carbonates and evaporites and Carboniferous–Permian coal measures. Magma intruded these rocks as sills and heated them, driving off carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide, methane and halogen compounds (chlorine and fluorine) in quantities far beyond what the magma itself would have degassed.

The consequences attributed to that release are global warming, ocean acidification, ocean anoxia and euxinia, destruction of the ozone layer, acid rain and metal poisoning. Together they are the accepted explanation for the severity of the extinction at the boundary.

Much of the lava is still there, exposed across the Putorana and Central Siberian plateaus, where it weathers into the stepped terraces that the word *trap* refers to.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_Traps).

name: Ichthyosaur radiation and dominance
summary: Dolphin-shaped marine reptiles that hunted the seas from the early Triassic until the Late Cretaceous.
body:
Ichthyosaurs were marine reptiles with a fish-like body: a fusiform trunk, a dorsal fin, paddle-shaped limbs and a vertical tail fin. They appear about 250 million years ago, early in the Triassic, and the last of them disappear around 94 million years ago in the Late Cretaceous.

They are a standard example of convergent evolution, having arrived from a terrestrial reptilian ancestor at a shape close to that of tuna and dolphins. Like whales they were air-breathing and bore live young, which is directly attested by fossils preserved in the act of giving birth. They had the largest eye sockets of any known vertebrate, which is usually read as an adaptation for hunting at depth or in low light.

Sizes ranged from about one metre to enormous. The Triassic *Shonisaurus* exceeded fifteen metres, and jaw fragments assigned to *Ichthyotitan* imply an animal of perhaps twenty-five.

They were the dominant marine reptiles of the Triassic and Early Jurassic, and afterwards shared the seas with plesiosaurs and, later, mosasaurs. Diversity fell in two steps during the Cenomanian, as specialised feeders disappeared and only generalist predators were left, before the group ended entirely. Mary Anning and her brother found the first complete ichthyosaur skull at Lyme Regis in 1811–12, among the earliest specimens described scientifically.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ichthyosaur).

name: First dinosaurs
summary: Small bipedal archosaurs from what is now Argentina mark the origin of the dinosaurian lineage.
body:
Dinosaurs originated in the Middle to Late Triassic, roughly twenty million years after the [end-Permian extinction](event:permian-extinction). The oldest substantial fossils come from the Ischigualasto Formation in north-western Argentina, dated to 231–230 million years ago, and from rocks of similar age in Brazil and Zimbabwe. *Herrerasaurus* and *Eoraptor* from Ischigualasto were bipedal and lightly built.

They were a minor part of Triassic land faunas, which were dominated by other archosaurs (the crocodile-line pseudosuchians), together with surviving [synapsids](event:synapsid-domination) and large amphibians. What distinguished dinosaurs anatomically was a hip socket open at its centre and a thigh bone with an inturned head, giving limbs held directly beneath the body rather than sprawling.

Their rise was a consequence of the [end-Triassic extinction](event:triassic-extinction) 201.4 million years ago, which removed most of the competing archosaur groups. Dinosaurs then dominated terrestrial ecosystems for the next 135 million years, through the Jurassic and the Cretaceous, reaching sizes no land animal has matched before or since.

The non-avian lineages ended at the [Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary](event:kpg-extinction) 66 million years ago. [Birds](event:first-birds), which are themselves dinosaurs, did not.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur).

name: First mammaliaforms
summary: The earliest mammals and related forms appeared as small animals during the rise of dinosaurian dominance.
body:
Mammaliaformes is the group containing mammals and their closest extinct relatives. Its members appear in the Late Triassic, around 205 million years ago, evolving from small cynodonts, the last surviving branch of the [synapsids](event:synapsid-domination) that had dominated the Permian.

They were shrew-sized. *Morganucodon*, known from thousands of specimens in fissure fillings in the limestone of South Wales and from China, was about ten centimetres long; *Hadrocodium*, from the Early Jurassic of China, was little more than three. Most were nocturnal insectivores, and their fossils are found alongside those of far larger [dinosaurs](event:first-dinosaurs).

What separates them from their ancestors is mostly internal. The teeth came to occlude precisely and were replaced only once, so that food could be chewed rather than merely gripped. The jaw joint moved to a new pair of bones, and two of the old jaw bones migrated into the middle ear, where they remain in every mammal. Patterns of tooth replacement in morganucodonts imply that the young were suckled, and preserved impressions show that fur was already present.

Small size and nocturnal habits persisted through the Mesozoic. Crown mammals (the group containing monotremes, marsupials and placentals) date from the Jurassic, with *Juramaia*, the earliest known eutherian, at about 160 million years. The pattern changed only after the [K–Pg extinction](event:kpg-extinction).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammaliaformes).

name: Triassic–Jurassic extinction
summary: Approximately 50% of known species went extinct during volcanic activity from the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province and Pangaea fragmentation.
body:
The Triassic–Jurassic extinction, 201.4 million years ago, is one of the five largest in the fossil record. Between 23 and 34 per cent of marine genera were lost, and about 42 per cent of terrestrial tetrapod species.

The conodonts, part of marine ecosystems since the Cambrian, were wiped out entirely. So were most ammonoid groups, particularly the ceratitids, and some 96 per cent of coral genera. On land the losses fell heavily on the groups that had shared the Triassic with the earliest [dinosaurs](event:first-dinosaurs): the large temnospondyl amphibians, and the crocodile-line archosaurs (phytosaurs, aetosaurs and rauisuchids), leaving only the ancestors of the crocodilians.

The cause is the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, an enormous flood basalt province erupted as [Pangaea](event:pangaea) began to rift along what became the [Atlantic](event:atlantic-opening). Carbon dioxide concentrations roughly quadrupled, producing rapid warming, ocean acidification and anoxia, along with a documented pulse of mercury.

Dinosaurs came through comparatively intact and radiated into the vacated niches within a few million years, which is why Jurassic faunas look so different from Triassic ones. Crocodylomorphs did much the same in the water.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triassic%E2%80%93Jurassic_extinction_event).

name: Opening of the Atlantic
summary: Rifting of Pangaea initiated the formation of a new ocean basin along the developing Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
body:
Part of [Pangaea supercontinent](event:pangaea). The Atlantic began as a rift in the interior of Pangaea and has been widening ever since. Rifting between North America and north-west Africa started in the Triassic and was producing ocean floor in the central Atlantic by about 175 million years ago; the South Atlantic opened from the Early Cretaceous as South America separated from Africa; the North Atlantic, between Greenland and Europe, opened last, 60 to 55 million years ago.

New crust is made along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a submarine mountain chain running the length of the ocean, where the plates pull apart and mantle material rises to fill the gap. The average spreading rate is about 2.5 centimetres a year. The ridge rises above sea level in Iceland, where the plate boundary can be walked across at Þingvellir.

The Atlantic sea floor supplied the decisive evidence for plate tectonics. Basalt records the direction of Earth's magnetic field as it cools, and the field reverses at irregular intervals, so the floor on either side of the ridge carries a matching, symmetrical pattern of magnetic stripes, mapped through the late 1950s and 1960s. Nowhere on Earth is there ocean floor much older than about 180 million years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean).

name: Sauropod gigantism and herbivory
summary: Quadrupedal dinosaurs achieved the largest body sizes known for terrestrial animals, reaching several tens of metric tonnes.
body:
Sauropods were quadrupedal, long-necked, long-tailed herbivorous dinosaurs, and they include the largest animals that have ever lived on land. Unequivocal sauropods appear in the Early Jurassic, the group reached its greatest diversity in the Late Jurassic around 150 million years ago, and titanosaurs remained abundant until the [end of the Cretaceous](event:kpg-extinction).

The largest are known only from partial skeletons, so mass estimates carry wide error bars. *Argentinosaurus* is reconstructed at 35 to 36 metres long and 65 to 80 tonnes; some *Barosaurus* material implies an animal longer still. Nineteenth-century claims for larger animals, such as *Amphicoelias fragillimus* at 58 metres, are now regarded as exaggerated or unverifiable.

Several features made the size possible. The bones of the neck and trunk were pneumatic (hollowed out by air sacs connected to the lungs), so that a very long neck need not be unliftably heavy. The head was small and simple, with peg-like or spoon-shaped teeth that cropped vegetation without chewing it and were replaced every few weeks; digestion happened in a very large gut instead. The limbs were pillar-like, and the animals grew fast and laid many small eggs rather than bearing a few large young.

*Brachiosaurus*, *Diplodocus* and *Apatosaurus* come from the Morrison Formation of the western United States; closely comparable animals are known from Tendaguru in Tanzania.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauropoda).

name: Theropod radiation and predatory dominance
summary: Bipedal carnivorous dinosaurs became the dominant apex predators, evolving from small forms to giants.
body:
Theropods were the bipedal, mostly carnivorous dinosaurs. They appear in the Late Triassic, about 231 million years ago, and were the dominant land predators for the rest of the Mesozoic. As birds, they remain the most species-rich group of land vertebrates.

The range of size within the group is extreme. *Anchiornis*, a feathered Jurassic form, weighed about 110 grams; *Tyrannosaurus*, *Giganotosaurus*, *Carcharodontosaurus* and *Spinosaurus* were all in the region of twelve metres and several tonnes. Living theropods run from the bee hummingbird at under two grams to the ostrich.

Feathers were not an avian invention. They are now known from across the coelurosaurs (the group that includes tyrannosaurs and *Velociraptor* as well as birds), in forms ranging from simple filaments to fully vaned flight feathers, and some large species appear to have lost them again. Hollow bones, wishbones, air-sac lungs, brooding of nests and three-fingered hands all appear in theropods well before flight does.

[Birds](event:first-birds) evolved from small coelurosaurs during the Jurassic, and are the only dinosaurs to have survived the [K–Pg extinction](event:kpg-extinction).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theropoda).

name: Archaeopteryx and the first birds
summary: Feathered theropods from the Jurassic lagoon deposits at Solnhofen record dinosaurs at an intermediate stage on the way to birds.
body:
*Archaeopteryx* is a small feathered dinosaur from the Solnhofen limestone of southern Germany, about 150 million years old, and the best-known transitional fossil between non-avian dinosaurs and birds. Fourteen body fossils are known, all from the same lagoon deposits; the first was described in 1861, two years after *On the Origin of Species*, and it has been central to arguments about transitional forms ever since.

It was about the size of a raven, up to half a metre long, with a wingspan around 70 centimetres and a mass between 500 grams and a kilogram. Its feathers are modern in structure and asymmetrical in the way flight feathers are; it had a wishbone and broad wings. It also had small teeth, a long bony tail, three clawed fingers on each hand and a hyperextensible second toe of the kind *Velociraptor* had.

Whether it counts as the earliest bird or as a close relative just outside the group has moved back and forth as feathered dinosaurs have been described from China and analyses rerun. The question is now about where a line is drawn rather than about what the animal was.

Birds are [dinosaurs](event:theropod-radiation), and the only lineage of them to survive the [end-Cretaceous extinction](event:kpg-extinction). About 11,000 species are alive today.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeopteryx).

name: Rise of flowering plants
summary: Flowering plants appeared and, through interactions with insect pollinators, became the dominant plant group globally.
body:
Flowering plants, or angiosperms, enclose their seeds within a carpel and reproduce through flowers. They appear suddenly and already diverse in the fossil record of the Early Cretaceous, around 130 million years ago, and by the end of the period they had replaced conifers as the dominant canopy trees over much of the world. About 300,000 species are known today, in 416 families, the great majority of all land plants.

Their fossil appearance and their molecular history do not agree. Genetic evidence places the divergence of the angiosperm lineage from other seed plants far earlier, possibly in the late Devonian around 365 million years ago, leaving a long interval with no accepted fossils in it.

That mismatch, and the speed of the radiation once it began, is what Darwin called an "abominable mystery" in a letter of 1879. The usual resolution invokes co-evolution with animal pollinators: nectar, scent and coloured petals buy directed transfer of pollen, and specialisation between a flower's shape and a pollinator's anatomy isolates populations from one another, so that new species form quickly. Enclosed seeds, faster life cycles and more efficient water transport are also cited.

Grasses, which are angiosperms, went on to restructure terrestrial ecosystems a second time in the [Miocene](event:miocene-grassland-expansion).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowering_plant).

name: Cretaceous greenhouse climate
summary: The Cretaceous was among Earth's warmest periods, with atmospheric CO2 levels several times higher than modern concentrations.
body:
The Cretaceous was one of the warmest intervals of the Phanerozoic, and the mid-Cretaceous, from about 120 to 90 million years ago, was its warmest phase. There were no permanent polar ice caps; forests grew within the Arctic and Antarctic circles, and shallow seas flooded large areas of the continents as sea level stood well above its present height.

Warmth peaked around 94 million years ago, at the Cenomanian–Turonian thermal maximum. Tropical sea-surface temperatures reached 30 to 42 °C, deep ocean water was 15 to 20 °C warmer than today, and mean annual temperatures at the poles exceeded 14 °C. Carbon dioxide concentrations of 1,000 to 1,400 parts per million are estimated for the mid-Cretaceous, sustained by unusually vigorous submarine volcanism along fast-spreading ridges and large oceanic plateaus.

Warm, sluggishly circulating oceans repeatedly ran short of oxygen. These oceanic anoxic events buried enormous quantities of organic carbon, and the source rocks they left behind account for a large share of the world's petroleum. Chalk, the rock the period is named for, accumulated across shelf seas such as the [Western Interior Seaway](event:cretaceous-seaway) from the skeletons of calcareous plankton.

Cooling had already begun in the Late Cretaceous when the [Chicxulub impact](event:chicxulub) ended the period.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous).

name: Cretaceous Western Interior Seaway
summary: A shallow inland sea extended from the Arctic to the Gulf of Mexico, hosting mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, and ammonites.
body:
The Western Interior Seaway was a shallow sea that split North America in two for most of the Late Cretaceous, from about 100 to 66 million years ago. At its greatest extent it ran more than 3,200 kilometres from the Arctic Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico, was up to 970 kilometres wide, and reached about 760 metres deep.

It formed as the crust east of the rising Laramide mountain belt was pushed down under the weight of it, and seawater transgressed south into the resulting basin. Warm and shallow, it laid down chalk and organic-rich shale over an enormous area.

Its fauna is among the best known of any Cretaceous sea.
