Mosasaurs and plesiosaurs were the large predators; the bony fish *Xiphactinus* reached four to five metres; ammonites, belemnites and inoceramid bivalves were abundant; and the flightless diving bird *Hesperornis* and the flying *Ichthyornis* lived along it, together with large pterosaurs. The Niobrara Chalk and Pierre Shale of Kansas, Nebraska and the Dakotas are the classic collecting grounds, with exposures such as Monument Rocks.

Continued Laramide uplift drained the seaway southwards, and it was gone by the early Paleocene.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Interior_Seaway).

name: Rise of eutherian mammals
summary: Small eutherians, the lineage leading to placental mammals, spread and diversified while dinosaurs dominated terrestrial ecosystems.
body:
Placental mammals, the group containing every living mammal except the monotremes and marsupials, carry their young in the uterus to a late stage of development, sustained by a placenta. The wider group they belong to, the eutherians, is much older than the placental orders themselves.

Eutherians are known from the Middle Jurassic, about 170 million years ago; *Juramaia* from China is the earliest. Through the Cretaceous they remained small, largely nocturnal insectivores, well represented in fossil assemblages from China and Mongolia but absent from any large-bodied role, since [dinosaurs](event:theropod-radiation) occupied those.

When the modern placental orders separated is disputed. Molecular clocks put the divergence of the three major placental lineages between about 120 and 105 million years ago, deep in the Cretaceous. The fossil record does not support that: the earliest undisputed placental fossils are at or just below the [Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary](event:kpg-extinction), with *Protungulatum* appearing a few hundred thousand years before it.

The reading now generally favoured is a short fuse, in which the lineages had originated and begun to diverge in the Late Cretaceous but their [radiation into large-bodied and diurnal roles](event:paleocene-mammal-radiation) came only once the extinction had removed the animals occupying them.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Placentalia).

name: Deccan Traps eruptions
summary: Flood basalt eruptions occurred in western India during the interval of the Chicxulub impact.
body:
The Deccan Traps are a flood basalt province covering about 500,000 square kilometres of west-central India, with a preserved volume near one million cubic kilometres; the original extent may have been three times as large. The stepped hills the lava flows weather into give the province its name.

Eruption spanned roughly 66.3 to 65.6 million years ago (600,000 to 800,000 years straddling the [Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary](event:kpg-extinction)), with the most intense phase possibly lasting less than 30,000 years. The source was the Réunion hotspot, a mantle plume that India was then passing over and that still builds volcanic islands in the Indian Ocean.

Because the eruptions coincide with the extinction, they were for a time proposed as its cause, or as a co-cause alongside the [Chicxulub impact](event:chicxulub). That view has lost ground. Sulphur dioxide from the eruptions is estimated to have cooled the planet by around 2 °C, which stresses ecosystems but does not by itself explain the pattern of losses, and climate modelling published in 2020 favoured the impact alone. Some recent work argues that volcanic carbon dioxide may even have shortened the impact winter.

Volcanic provinces of this scale have been implicated in other mass extinctions, most clearly the [Siberian Traps](event:siberian-traps) at the end of the Permian.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deccan_Traps).

name: Chicxulub impact
summary: A 10-kilometre-diameter asteroid impacted the Yucatán platform, releasing energy equivalent to billions of Hiroshima bombs.
body:
Part of [Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction](event:kpg-extinction). The Chicxulub crater lies buried beneath the northern Yucatán Peninsula and the sea floor off it, centred near the town of Chicxulub Puerto. It is 180 to 200 kilometres across and about a kilometre below younger sediment, and it was made 66 million years ago by an asteroid roughly ten kilometres in diameter, most probably a carbonaceous chondrite from beyond Jupiter's orbit.

Estimates of the energy released span two orders of magnitude, from tens of millions to billions of megatonnes of TNT equivalent, with winds above 1,000 kilometres an hour near the site. What made it globally lethal, however, was the target: the platform is thick carbonate and sulphur-rich gypsum, and vaporising them injected carbon dioxide and enormous quantities of sulphate aerosol into the stratosphere, where they blocked sunlight and later fell as acid rain.

It was found by accident. Glen Penfield and Antonio Camargo identified a buried circular magnetic and gravity anomaly during petroleum exploration in 1978, and their interpretation went largely unnoticed until Alan Hildebrand made contact in 1990; drill samples containing shock-metamorphic minerals confirmed it, and the identification was published in 1991. In 2016 a joint expedition drilled the offshore peak ring to 1,335 metres below the sea floor, recovering rock that had been fluidised by the impact and thrown back inward.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicxulub_crater).

name: Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction
summary: Approximately 75% of all species, including all non-avian dinosaurs, went extinct during a geologically brief interval.
body:
The Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction, 66 million years ago, ended the Mesozoic era and killed about three-quarters of the plant and animal species on Earth. All non-avian dinosaurs died, along with the pterosaurs, the mosasaurs and plesiosaurs, the ammonites and most of the calcareous plankton. Almost no land animal heavier than about 25 kilograms survived.

The cause is the impact of an asteroid at [Chicxulub](event:chicxulub) on the Yucatán platform. The first evidence was chemical: a thin clay layer at the boundary, found worldwide, containing far more iridium than Earth's crust normally holds but about as much as a meteorite. Shocked quartz, glass spherules and then a crater of the right age and size followed.

The immediate mechanism was the loss of sunlight. Dust and sulphate aerosols from vaporised rock spread through the stratosphere and shut down photosynthesis for months to years, collapsing food chains on land and in the surface ocean. Wildfires, a pulse of acid rain and megatsunamis exceeding a hundred metres in shallow seas added to it. The [Deccan Traps](event:deccan-traps) were erupting at the same time and had already been altering the climate, though modelling now assigns them a secondary role.

Survival was selective in ways that make sense of that mechanism. Small burrowing and semi-aquatic animals came through better than large surface-dwelling ones, and freshwater communities, which run on detritus rather than on living plants, did far better than terrestrial and marine ones dependent on photosynthesis. Among tetrapods the survivors were [birds](event:first-birds), crocodilians, turtles, lizards, snakes, amphibians and [mammals](event:paleocene-mammal-radiation).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous%E2%80%93Paleogene_extinction_event).

name: Paleocene mammalian radiation
summary: After dinosaur extinction, mammals increased rapidly in taxonomic diversity and body size, occupying newly vacant ecological roles.
body:
Part of [Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction](event:kpg-extinction). The Paleocene, from 66 to 56 million years ago, is the ten-million-year interval in which the world reassembled after the extinction and mammals moved into the roles that had been vacated.

Plant communities recovered first, in a documented sequence: an immediate spike of fern spores directly above the boundary clay, then pioneering species, then slowly diversifying forests that stayed species-poor for most of the epoch. The climate was a greenhouse one, with no permanent polar ice and global mean temperatures around 24 to 25 °C.

Average mammal body size increased sharply above the boundary and kept increasing. Within a few million years there were herbivores the size of sheep and larger (the archaic hoofed condylarths, the bulky pantodonts), along with the carnivorous mammals that hunted them, and the first plesiadapiforms, close relatives of the primates. The sequence is exceptionally well recorded in the Bighorn Basin of Wyoming, where successive faunas are stacked in continuous sediment. Birds also radiated quickly, and included large flightless predators.

The epoch ends abruptly at the [Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum](event:petm), after which the modern orders of hoofed mammals and primates are all present.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleocene).

name: Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum
summary: A large carbon input to the atmosphere caused global warming of 5–8 °C within several thousand years.
body:
The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum was an episode of rapid global warming about 56 million years ago. Global temperatures rose by 5 to 8 °C, tropical sea surfaces exceeded 36 °C, and the whole event (onset, peak and recovery) lasted roughly 200,000 years.

It is identified by a sharp negative excursion in carbon isotopes recorded in marine and terrestrial carbonates at more than 130 sites worldwide. A shift of that kind requires the addition of a very large quantity of carbon depleted in carbon-13 to the ocean and atmosphere; estimates run into thousands of gigatonnes. Candidate sources include volcanic carbon from the North Atlantic Igneous Province, dissociation of methane hydrates on the sea floor, and the cooking of organic-rich sediment by intruding magma.

The ocean acidified, and carbonate that had been accumulating on the deep sea floor dissolved. Between 35 and 50 per cent of deep-sea benthic foraminifera became extinct within about a thousand years, the largest deep-ocean extinction of the Cenozoic. On land, mammal faunas turned over rapidly: several modern orders, among them the artiodactyls, perissodactyls and primates, appear and spread across the northern continents at this point, and many lineages became temporarily smaller.

It is the closest geological analogue to present-day [greenhouse warming](event:global-warming), although carbon is being released today several times faster than it was during the PETM.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleocene%E2%80%93Eocene_Thermal_Maximum).

name: Early Eocene Climatic Optimum
summary: The warmest sustained interval of the Cenozoic, with no polar ice and forests growing inside the Arctic Circle.
body:
The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, from about 54 to 49 million years ago, was the warmest sustained interval of the Cenozoic. It followed a series of shorter warming events, of which the [PETM](event:petm) was the largest, and it is the peak of the greenhouse world that preceded the long cooling towards the present ice-age climate.

There was no permanent ice at either pole. Tropical sea-surface temperatures have been reconstructed at 36 °C and above, and deep ocean water was far warmer than today. Tropical forest extended into what is now northern North America and Europe, palms grew in Alaska, and forests of swamp cypress and dawn redwood covered Ellesmere Island inside the Arctic Circle, where crocodilians and turtles also lived. Carbon dioxide concentrations were several times the pre-industrial level.

Mammals of the early Eocene were small (around 60 per cent of the size of their Paleocene predecessors), and it is in this interval that the oldest fossils of most modern mammal orders appear.

Cooling set in from about 49 million years ago and continued, helped by the carbon burial of the Azolla event in the Arctic and by the drawdown of carbon dioxide through [Himalayan](event:himalaya-uplift) weathering, until [Antarctica glaciated](event:antarctic-glaciation) 34 million years ago.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Eocene_Climatic_Optimum).

name: Whale evolution from terrestrial mammals
summary: Artiodactyl mammals returned to marine environments and evolved into fully aquatic cetaceans.
body:
Whales evolved from land mammals during the Eocene, and the sequence is one of the most completely documented transitions in the fossil record. Their ancestors were even-toed ungulates; the closest living relatives of whales are hippopotamuses, with which they last shared an ancestor about 55 million years ago.

The stages are known largely from rocks in Pakistan and India, laid down along the shore of the closing Tethys. *Pakicetus*, about 50 million years old, was a wading freshwater animal, recognisable as a cetacean only from the structure of its ear bones. *Ambulocetus*, some 49 million years old, was a crocodile-like predator of bays and estuaries. The remingtonocetids and protocetids that follow are progressively more marine: eyes reduced, nostrils migrating back along the skull, and the semicircular canals of the inner ear shrinking to the small size typical of fully aquatic animals, a change regarded as a point of no return. Protocetids such as *Rodhocetus* and *Maiacetus* spread beyond Asia to Africa, Europe and North America; a *Maiacetus* fossil preserving a foetus positioned head-first suggests that birth still took place on land.

The first obligate swimmers are the basilosaurids of the late Eocene, 41 to 34 million years ago. They include *Basilosaurus*, long-bodied and with vestigial hind limbs, and the smaller *Dorudon*, both well represented at Wadi Al-Hitan in Egypt. The two modern groups, the baleen and the toothed whales, separated around 34 to 28 million years ago, and echolocation appears with the latter.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolution_of_cetaceans).

name: Uplift of the Himalaya
summary: Collision of the Indian plate with Asian continental crust produced the world's highest mountain range and altered global climate.
body:
The Himalaya are the product of a continental collision that began about 55 million years ago, when the northward-moving Indian plate met Eurasia and the ocean between them closed. Neither plate could be subducted, so the crust thickened and rose. The range now runs 2,400 kilometres in an arc from the Indus to the Brahmaputra, with more than a hundred peaks above 7,200 metres and Mount Everest at 8,848.86 metres.

The collision has not finished. India still moves north at about 67 millimetres a year, of which some 20 are absorbed by thrusting along the southern front of the range; the mountains rise about 5 millimetres a year, and around 7 at the syntaxes at either end, where the arc bends sharply. Great earthquakes on the frontal thrusts are the direct consequence.

The range has a large effect on the climate of Asia. It blocks cold northerly air from reaching the subcontinent and forces the summer monsoon to rise and drop its moisture on the southern slopes, leaving arid basins and deserts (the Taklamakan, the Gobi) in the rain shadow beyond.

Uplift on this scale also exposes enormous quantities of fresh silicate rock to chemical weathering, which consumes atmospheric carbon dioxide. That drawdown is one of the standard explanations for the long Cenozoic cooling that ended in the [Quaternary ice ages](event:quaternary-ice-ages).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas).

name: Antarctica freezes
summary: Declining atmospheric CO2 and opening of the Drake Passage enabled permanent ice sheet formation at the South Pole.
body:
A permanent ice sheet formed over Antarctica about 34 million years ago, at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary. The event marks the change from the greenhouse world that had prevailed since the [Cretaceous](event:cretaceous-warmth) to the icehouse world that has held ever since, and ice has been present on the continent from that point to the present.

The principal cause was falling atmospheric carbon dioxide. Modelling places the threshold for continental glaciation near 600 parts per million, and levels crossed it during the late Eocene; a favourable orbital configuration set the timing of the onset itself, in a step known as the Oi-1 event.

The opening of the ocean gateways around Antarctica (the Tasman Gateway and the Drake Passage) allowed the Antarctic Circumpolar Current to establish itself and thermally isolate the continent. This was long regarded as the main cause, and models now generally give it a supporting role behind carbon dioxide.

The ice sheet today covers 98 per cent of Antarctica, some 14 million square kilometres, averages more than two kilometres thick and holds 26.5 million cubic kilometres of ice: about 61 per cent of the world's fresh water, and the equivalent of roughly 53 metres of sea level.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_ice_sheet).

name: Oligocene transition and global cooling
summary: Climate shifted from warm and humid to cooler and more arid conditions over millions of years.
body:
Part of [Antarctica freezes](event:antarctic-glaciation). The Oligocene, from 33.9 to 23 million years ago, was cooler and drier than anything before it in the Cenozoic. Global temperature fell by 5 to 6 °C across the Eocene–Oligocene transition, and by the end of that transition the world's ice was about a quarter more extensive than today's.

The epoch opens with a faunal turnover in Europe known as the Grande Coupure, when the retreat of the Obik Sea across western Siberia opened a land connection and Asian mammals replaced much of the endemic European fauna.

Falling temperature and falling carbon dioxide together pushed vegetation away from closed forest. Tropical forest contracted towards the equator while open woodland, scrub and the first extensive grasslands spread through the middle latitudes. Grasses using the C4 photosynthetic pathway, which is more efficient where carbon dioxide is scarce, appear during this interval.

Mammal faunas changed accordingly, and most modern families are recognisable by the end of the epoch. Body sizes were generally small, with conspicuous exceptions such as *Paraceratherium*, a hornless rhinoceros relative and the largest land mammal known. The trend continued into the [Miocene](event:miocene-grassland-expansion), when grasslands became a dominant biome in their own right.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oligocene).

name: Miocene grassland expansion
summary: Grassland vegetation expanded across continents, restructuring terrestrial ecosystems toward grazing-based food webs.
body:
Grasslands spread across every inhabited continent during the Miocene, 23 to 5.3 million years ago, and in doing so restructured terrestrial ecosystems around grazing.

The epoch began warm, with the Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum around 16 million years ago and carbon dioxide between 300 and 500 parts per million, and then cooled, sharply during the Late Miocene Cooling between about 7 and 5.3 million years ago, when ocean temperatures reached near-modern values. Cooler, drier and more seasonal conditions favoured grasses over trees. Grasses using the C4 photosynthetic pathway, which tolerates low carbon dioxide and high temperatures, became ecologically important between about 7 and 6 million years ago.

Grass is abrasive: it accumulates silica, and a grazing animal takes in grit with it. The response among herbivores was hypsodonty (high-crowned teeth with a long reserve of enamel), which evolved repeatedly in horses, antelopes, camels and rhinoceroses. Longer legs and life in herds belong to the same package, since open country offers no cover. Lineages that could not make the shift declined.

Africa's savannas date from this transition, and so does much of the context for [ape and hominin evolution](event:hominin-split): around a hundred ape species lived across Africa, Asia and Europe during the Miocene, and the hominin lineage separates from that of chimpanzees near its close.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miocene).

name: Human–chimpanzee divergence
summary: The hominin and chimpanzee lineages diverged in Africa.
body:
The hominin lineage, the branch leading to modern humans, separated from the branch leading to chimpanzees and bonobos in Africa in the late Miocene. The date is estimated from the number of genetic differences between the living species and the rate at which such differences accumulate, and it has moved as those rates have been re-measured: recent whole-genome analyses give 6.3 to 5.5 million years ago, while other studies allow a range from about 13 to 4.7 million.

No fossil has been identified with confidence as the last common ancestor, and the candidates near the divergence are all contested. *Sahelanthropus tchadensis*, from Chad and about 7 million years old, has a skull base that has been read as indicating upright posture, but it may equally be a Miocene ape with convergent features. *Orrorin tugenensis*, from Kenya and about 6 million years old, has a thigh bone with features shared with later hominins. *Ardipithecus*, at around 5.5 to 4.4 million years, most probably postdates the split.

Part of the difficulty is that speciation is not an event. The two lineages appear to have continued exchanging genes for some time after they began to separate, so the question of when they split has no single answer.

What follows in the hominin line is [habitual bipedalism](event:lucy), well before any enlargement of the brain.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimpanzee%E2%80%93human_last_common_ancestor).

name: Messinian salinity crisis
summary: The Mediterranean basin became isolated from the Atlantic and underwent extensive evaporation, leaving kilometre-thick salt deposits.
body:
The Messinian salinity crisis was the near-total desiccation of the Mediterranean between 5.96 and 5.33 million years ago. Tectonic movement along the Gibraltar arc restricted and then closed the connection to the Atlantic; with evaporation far exceeding what the rivers supplied, the sea shrank into hypersaline lakes lying kilometres below global sea level.

The result is a body of salt beneath the Mediterranean floor amounting to more than a million cubic kilometres, around fifty times the salt dissolved in the sea today. Glacio-eustatic sea-level changes worked with the tectonics: falls during northern hemisphere cooling deepened the isolation, and brief reconnections refilled the basin repeatedly before the final closure at about 5.6 million years ago, after which the basin is thought to have dried out within a thousand years.

It ended with the Zanclean flood at 5.33 million years ago, when the Atlantic broke back through at Gibraltar. Early reconstructions had this happening catastrophically, in as little as a couple of years; more recent work argues for a less violent and more gradual reflooding, and the question is open.

Marine life in the Mediterranean was largely wiped out and recolonised from the Atlantic afterwards, which is why its fauna is a depleted version of the Atlantic's. Land animals that crossed to islands while the basin was dry (in the Balearics, for instance) were left isolated there for the following five million years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messinian_salinity_crisis).

name: First stone tools
summary: Hominins began deliberately producing stone cutting tools, initiating the archaeological record.
body:
The deliberate flaking of stone to make cutting edges is where the archaeological record begins. The oldest claimed tools come from Lomekwi 3, west of Lake Turkana in Kenya, and are dated to 3.3 million years ago; they are large and heavy, struck by techniques unlike what follows, and whether they represent a tradition continuous with later toolmaking has not been established.

The first widespread industry is the Oldowan, which now reaches back to about 2.9 million years ago at Nyayanga in Kenya, with well-known assemblages from Gona in Ethiopia at 2.6 million and from Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, where Louis Leakey found the first examples in the 1930s. The technique is simple (a few flakes struck from a cobble with a hammerstone), but the flakes cut well, and the cores were used too.

Who made them is unsettled. They are conventionally attributed to early *Homo*, but the oldest examples predate the genus, and *Australopithecus garhi* and *Paranthropus* have both been proposed. More than one lineage may have been making them.

What the tools gave access to was meat and, by breaking bones, marrow, foods rich in energy and otherwise very hard for a primate to obtain. Cut-marked bones appear alongside them, and the change in diet is generally connected to the later increase in brain size. The [Acheulean hand-axe](event:hand-axe-tool-tradition) follows about 1.76 million years ago.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldowan).

name: Australopithecus and habitual bipedalism
summary: The Lucy skeleton showed that upright walking evolved millions of years before the enlargement of the human brain.
body:
Part of [Human–chimpanzee divergence](event:hominin-split). Lucy is a partial skeleton of *Australopithecus afarensis*, catalogued AL 288-1, found on 24 November 1974 by Donald Johanson and Tom Gray at Hadar in the Afar region of Ethiopia. About 40 per cent of one individual was recovered (several hundred fragments, with no bone duplicated), and volcanic ash layers bracketing the fossil date it to about 3.2 million years ago.

She stood roughly 1.1 metres tall and weighed around 29 kilograms. The pelvis, the inward-angled knee and the curvature of the lower spine show that she walked upright habitually, while the brain was about the size of a chimpanzee's. That combination established that bipedalism came first in human evolution and brain enlargement long afterwards, reversing an older assumption.

Trails of footprints preserved in volcanic ash at Laetoli in Tanzania, about 3.66 million years old, record the same kind of walking (a heel-strike gait with the big toe in line rather than splayed), made by animals of the same species.

The skeleton is named after a Beatles song played at the camp on the night it was found. Australopiths of this kind are the population from which [the first stone toolmakers](event:stone-tools) and, later, the genus *Homo* emerged.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_(Australopithecus)).

name: Quaternary ice ages begin
summary: Northern hemisphere ice sheets advanced and retreated repeatedly on orbital time scales.
body:
The Quaternary glaciation began 2.58 million years ago and is still in progress: the present is an interglacial within it, not a time outside it. Northern hemisphere ice sheets have grown and collapsed repeatedly through the period, while Antarctica has stayed glaciated throughout.

The rhythm is set by variations in Earth's orbit, the Milankovitch cycles. Eccentricity varies on a period near 100,000 years, axial tilt between about 22 and 24.5 degrees on 41,000 years, and precession on roughly 26,000. None of these changes the total sunlight the Earth receives by much; what they change is its distribution across seasons and latitudes, and what matters is whether northern summers are cool enough to leave the previous winter's snow unmelted.

For the first million and a half years the cycles followed the 41,000-year tilt period. After the Mid-Pleistocene Transition, about a million years ago, they lengthened to roughly 100,000 years and grew much larger in amplitude, for reasons still debated. Eight complete cycles have run in the last 740,000 years.

At their maxima the ice sheets were at least four kilometres thick and sea level stood about 120 metres lower than today. They ground down and rebuilt the landscapes of northern Europe, Canada and Siberia, and left millions of lakes behind them, among them the Great Lakes and the Baltic. The whole of hominin evolution and dispersal has taken place within this climate regime.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary_glaciation).

name: Homo erectus spreads out of Africa
summary: The first hominin with modern body proportions, ranging from Africa to Java and northern China.
body:
*Homo erectus* was the first hominin with essentially modern body proportions: long legs, short arms, a narrow pelvis and a barrel chest, built for walking and running over distance rather than for climbing. It appeared in Africa around 2 million years ago and is the first human species known to have left it.

Its range was enormous. Fossils at Dmanisi in Georgia date to 1.85 to 1.78 million years ago; sites in Java, including Sangiran and Mojokerto, to between 1.8 and 1.6 million; and Zhoukoudian near Beijing, source of the Peking Man material, is younger again. In Africa the best-known specimen is the Turkana Boy, a nearly complete juvenile skeleton from Kenya.

Adults stood between about 1.4 and 1.7 metres and weighed around 50 kilograms. Brain volume varied widely across the species' range and its two-million-year span, from well under 1,000 cubic centimetres in early African specimens to about 1,000 in East Asian ones, above the australopiths and below modern humans. The species is associated with the [Acheulean hand-axe](event:hand-axe-tool-tradition) industry in Africa and western Eurasia, though East Asian populations went on using simpler choppers, and with the earliest and most contested evidence for [fire](event:fire-control).

The last known populations, in Java, date to between about 117,000 and 108,000 years ago. Nearly two million years is the longest span documented for any human species.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus).

name: Acheulean hand-axe tradition
summary: Symmetrical stone hand-axes produced by early humans are found across Africa, Europe, and Asia.
body:
Part of [First stone tools](event:stone-tools). The Acheulean is the stone tool industry defined by the hand-axe: a large oval or pear-shaped core worked on both faces to a symmetrical edge running most of the way around it. It appears about 1.76 million years ago at Kokiselei in West Turkana, Kenya (with a 2023 claim from Ethiopia at 1.95 million), and it persisted, with modifications, for well over a million years.

Making one means roughing out the shape with a hammerstone and then finishing it with a softer hammer of bone, antler or wood, which detaches thinner flakes with more control. That is a sequence of operations carried out towards a form the maker must already have in mind, and the standardisation of that form across Africa, western Asia, South Asia and Europe is the first unambiguous archaeological evidence of planning and of a transmitted technique.

The earliest makers were *Homo ergaster*, that is early [*Homo erectus*](event:homo-erectus); later users included *Homo heidelbergensis* and early [Neanderthals](event:neanderthals). East Asian assemblages of comparable age are mostly simpler choppers, and why that is has been argued over for decades.

What hand-axes were for is not settled either. Butchery is the usual answer, with digging, woodworking and use as a portable source of flakes also proposed. Prepared-core techniques displaced the Acheulean in Europe and the Middle East by about 125,000 years ago, and it survived latest in East Asia.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acheulean).

name: Control of fire
summary: Hominins developed the ability to produce and maintain fire, affecting diet, safety, and social organisation.
body:
The control of fire gave early humans cooked food, warmth, protection from predators and light after dark. When it began is among the harder questions in palaeoanthropology, because the traces fire leaves are easily produced by natural burning and easily destroyed.

The earliest claims are contested. Burnt bone and ashed plant material from Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, found deep inside the cave and identified by micromorphology and infrared spectroscopy, are dated between about 1.8 and 1.0 million years ago. Reddened sediment at Koobi Fora in Kenya, consistent with heating to 200–400 °C, is around 1.5 million years old. Neither is universally accepted, and most evidence for controlled fire in the Lower Palaeolithic is regarded as uncertain.

Firmer evidence comes later. Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in Israel, about 780,000 years old, preserves repeatedly used hearth areas and burnt fish teeth in a pattern that indicates cooking. From 400,000 to 300,000 years ago hearths become common and unambiguous across Europe, western Asia and Africa; by around 125,000 years ago fire use is effectively universal among anatomically modern humans.

The cooking hypothesis holds that fire's main effect was nutritional: cooked food yields more usable energy for less chewing and less gut, which would help pay for a large brain. Critics point out that the archaeological timing fits the expansion of the brain poorly, and that fire's other benefits (warmth, protection from predators, light after dark) do not depend on cooking at all.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_of_fire_by_early_humans).

name: Origin of Homo sapiens
summary: Anatomically modern humans originated in Africa, with the oldest known fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco.
body:
*Homo sapiens* emerged in Africa at least 300,000 years ago. The oldest fossils generally assigned to the species come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco and are about 315,000 years old: the face is essentially modern, while the braincase is still long and low. Omo Kibish in Ethiopia, at about 233,000 years, provides the oldest anatomically modern skeleton, and Herto and Florisbad add further early material.

The picture that has replaced a single point of origin is a pan-African one. Different populations across the continent carried different combinations of modern and archaic features, and gene flow between them, over tens of thousands of years and thousands of kilometres, assembled the modern form, rather than any one lineage evolving it in isolation. The molecular evidence fits: the most recent common ancestor of living mitochondrial lineages dates to roughly 148,000 to 99,000 years ago and of Y chromosomes to 156,000 to 120,000, both long after the species itself appears.

Behavioural modernity (pigments, ornaments, composite tools, long-distance transport of raw material, systematic use of marine resources) accumulates over a long period, from perhaps 160,000 years ago onward, rather than arriving all at once.

Early excursions out of Africa are documented at Misliya Cave in Israel between 194,000 and 177,000 years ago and at Skhul and Qafzeh between 120,000 and 100,000, with a contested claim at Apidima in Greece around 210,000. None of those populations left descendants. The [dispersal that populated the world](event:out-of-africa) came later, between about 70,000 and 50,000 years ago, and by then *Homo sapiens* shared the planet with [Neanderthals](event:neanderthals), [Denisovans](event:denisovans) and at least two other human species.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_sapiens).

name: Denisovan presence in Asia
summary: A human species related to Neanderthals ranged across Siberia, Central Asia, and into tropical regions, with DNA sequences preserved in modern Oceanian populations.
body:
The Denisovans are an extinct group of archaic humans, sister to the [Neanderthals](event:neanderthals), that ranged across Asia from roughly 200,000 to 32,000 years ago. They are unusual in having been identified from DNA before they were described from bones: the first evidence, published in 2010, was a genome sequenced from a juvenile finger bone excavated in 2008 at Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains of southern Siberia.

Physical remains are still sparse and scattered. Denisova Cave has yielded fragments dated between about 195,000 and 51,600 years ago. A mandible from Baishiya Karst Cave on the Tibetan Plateau is more than 160,000 years old; a tooth from Tam Ngu Hao 2 in Laos is 164,000 to 131,000; a jaw dredged from the Penghu Channel off Taiwan is 190,000 to 130,000; and the Harbin cranium from north-east China, over 146,000 years old, has been assigned to them on protein and DNA evidence. The range therefore runs from Siberia and high Tibet to the tropics.

They interbred with modern humans during the [dispersal out of Africa](event:out-of-africa). Denisovan ancestry accounts for roughly 5 per cent of the genomes of Papuans, Aboriginal Australians and Philippine Negritos, and about 0.2 per cent in mainland Asians and Native Americans. At least one inherited variant is demonstrably functional: the version of the EPAS1 gene that helps Tibetans tolerate low oxygen at altitude came from them.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denisovan).

name: Homo sapiens African diversification
summary: Anatomically modern humans dispersed throughout Africa, with populations interacting and exchanging genetic material.
body:
Part of [Origin of Homo sapiens](event:homo-sapiens). Between roughly 200,000 and 100,000 years ago modern humans were an African species, living in populations that were separated for long stretches and then exchanged genes again.

The fossils of this interval come from widely scattered places and do not converge on any one region: Omo Kibish and Herto in Ethiopia, Florisbad and Klasies River in South Africa, Ngaloba in Tanzania. Reconstructions of ancient African population structure from modern genomes point the same way, to a set of subdivided populations connected by intermittent migration rather than to a single ancestral group in a single place.

That is the model, sometimes called African multiregionalism or a structured pan-African origin, which has largely replaced the idea of one small founding population. Modern anatomy and modern behaviour did not appear together in one lineage; they were assembled from features that arose in different places and spread by gene flow.

The consequence for what came afterwards is that the [population that left Africa](event:out-of-africa) carried only a fraction of the species' variation. African populations remain the most genetically diverse in the world, and every non-African population descends from that narrow sample.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recent_African_origin_of_modern_humans).

name: Homo floresiensis on Flores
summary: A small-bodied human species persisted on an Indonesian island, possibly derived from *Homo erectus*.
body:
*Homo floresiensis* was a small-bodied human species that lived on the Indonesian island of Flores. The first remains were excavated from Liang Bua cave on 2 September 2003, and the skeletal material there is now dated between about 100,000 and 60,000 years ago, with associated stone tools ranging from 190,000 to 50,000.

An adult stood roughly 1.1 metres tall and weighed around 25 kilograms. The most complete individual, LB1, had a brain volume of about 380 cubic centimetres, comparable to a chimpanzee's and less than half that of *Homo erectus*, from which the species probably derives. More than 10,000 stone artefacts have been recovered from the cave, including flakes, points, blades and perforators, and there is disputed evidence for the hunting of juvenile *Stegodon*, a dwarf elephant relative that shared the island.

The small size was at first explained as pathology in a modern human (microcephaly, Down syndrome and iodine deficiency were all proposed), and those explanations have been rejected: detailed analysis found no pathology, and older fossils from Mata Menge elsewhere on Flores, about 700,000 years old, show the same small size in an earlier population. Island dwarfing, a common response among large mammals isolated where resources are limited, is the accepted account.

Modern humans reached the region around 50,000 years ago, at about the point the species disappears from the record.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_floresiensis).

name: Toba supereruption
summary: The largest known volcanic eruption of the last two million years deposited ash across South Asia.
body:
The Youngest Toba eruption, about 74,000 years ago at what is now Lake Toba in Sumatra, was the largest explosive volcanic eruption of the Quaternary. Argon-argon dating gives 73,880 ± 320 years. It reached the top of the volcanic explosivity index, at 8, and ejected an estimated 3,800 cubic kilometres of material, some 1,800 as ash fall and 2,000 as ignimbrite.

Its ash is a marker horizon across more than 38 million square kilometres. A layer five centimetres thick was laid down across the Indian subcontinent, and three and a half centimetres in the South China Sea.

The eruption became widely known through the Toba catastrophe hypothesis, put forward in the 1990s: that the volcanic winter it caused lasted six to ten years, was followed by a thousand-year cold period, and cut the human population to a few thousand individuals, leaving a bottleneck visible in modern DNA.

That hypothesis is no longer supported. Climate modelling gives a maximum global cooling of about 3.5 °C, returning to within the range of natural variability roughly five years after the eruption. Sediment cores from Lake Malawi show no volcanic winter in East Africa at the time, and archaeological sequences in South Africa run through the ash layer without interruption. The eruption was very large, but its effect on human populations appears to have been far smaller than the hypothesis claimed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youngest_Toba_eruption).

name: Out of Africa dispersal
summary: Modern humans dispersed from Africa and colonized every habitable continent within tens of thousands of years.
body:
The dispersal out of Africa is the expansion, between about 70,000 and 50,000 years ago, that put modern humans on every habitable continent. Every population living outside Africa today descends from it. The founding group was small (genetic evidence points to a few thousand people at most, carrying mitochondrial haplogroup L3), and it most probably crossed at the southern end of the Red Sea, at Bab-el-Mandeb, or overland through Sinai.

It was not the first attempt. Modern humans reached the Levant at Misliya Cave 194,000 to 177,000 years ago and at Skhul and Qafzeh 120,000 to 100,000 years ago, and there are early finds in Arabia and possibly Greece. None of those populations left descendants in the modern gene pool.

Along the way the dispersing population met and interbred with the archaic humans already in Eurasia. About 2 per cent of the genome of every non-African alive today is [Neanderthal](event:neanderthals), from admixture dated between roughly 65,000 and 47,000 years ago, and [Denisovan](event:denisovans) ancestry runs from 0.2 per cent in mainland Asia to around 5 per cent in New Guinea and Aboriginal Australia.

The expansion was rapid. [Australia](event:sahul) was reached by 65,000 to 50,000 years ago, across open water; Europe by 45,000; Siberia by 40,000 and the Russian Arctic by 27,000; and [the Americas](event:americas-peopling), the last continents, by about 16,000 years ago. The steps below follow that sequence.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_human_migrations).

steps.name: Crossing into Eurasia
steps.page:
A population carrying mitochondrial haplogroup L3 leaves north-east Africa, most probably by way of the Bab-el-Mandeb strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, where the crossing is narrowest and sea level during a glacial period stood far lower than today. An overland route through Sinai and the Levant is the alternative, and the two are not exclusive.

The genetic signal is of a founder group small enough that the whole of non-African humanity carries a subset of African variation. The route beyond the crossing is usually reconstructed as a southern one, along the coasts of Arabia, Iran and South Asia, which is also the fastest way to reach [Sahul](event:sahul).

steps.name: Arrival in Europe
steps.page:
Modern humans are securely present in Europe from about 45,000 years ago, with early sites in Bulgaria, Italy and Germany; some of the earliest individuals sequenced carry Neanderthal ancestry from interbreeding only a few generations back. They arrive into a continent occupied by [Neanderthals](event:neanderthals) and share it with them for several thousand years.

The Upper Palaeolithic industries belong to this period (blades struck from prepared cores, bone and antler points, eyed needles), and so do the earliest European [painted caves](event:cave-art).

name: Peopling of Australia
summary: Humans crossed open ocean to reach Sahul, the combined landmass of Australia and New Guinea.
body:
Part of [Out of Africa dispersal](event:out-of-africa). Sahul was the single landmass formed by Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania when sea level was low, and reaching it required a genuine sea voyage. Even at the glacial minimum the island chain between Sunda and Sahul left crossings of tens of kilometres of open water, with a shortest leg of around 90 kilometres and the destination not visible from the departure point.

Estimates for the arrival cluster between 65,000 and 50,000 years ago. The Madjedbebe rock shelter in Arnhem Land has produced artefacts dated by optically stimulated luminescence to about 65,000 years; the reliability of that date has been questioned, and genomic evidence for the ancestry of living Aboriginal Australians tends to support a somewhat later arrival, after about 50,000 years ago.

Two broad routes through Wallacea have been proposed: a northern one by way of Sulawesi to New Guinea, and a southern one by way of Timor to north-western Australia. Either way, the people who made the crossing were among the earliest mariners known anywhere.

The oldest human remains on the continent are from Lake Mungo in New South Wales, about 41,000 years old, and include a cremation. Around sixty species of Australian [large marsupials, birds and reptiles](event:megafauna-pleistocene) disappear from about 46,000 years ago, and how much of that was caused by people is still argued.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistory_of_Australia).

name: Pleistocene megafauna diversity
summary: Large ice-age animals such as mammoths, giant ground sloths and cave bears inhabited the continents during the Pleistocene.
body:
Megafauna, conventionally land animals over about 45 kilograms, were far more diverse during the Pleistocene than they are now. Mammoths and mastodons, woolly rhinoceroses, giant ground sloths, glyptodonts, cave bears, sabre-toothed cats, dire wolves, giant kangaroos and wombats, moa and elephant birds all lived alongside modern humans.

Most of them disappeared in a wave of extinctions running from about 50,000 to 10,000 years ago, unevenly across the continents. Sahul lost around 88 per cent of its megafaunal species by roughly 50,000 years ago; North America 72 per cent between 13,800 and 11,400 years ago; South America 83 per cent by about 13,000. Northern Eurasia lost its megafauna in a longer, staggered sequence, while Africa and southern Asia lost comparatively little. In total about 65 per cent of megafaunal species went, and around 80 per cent of mammals over a tonne.

Two explanations compete. The overkill hypothesis notes that the extinctions follow the arrival of modern humans on each landmass, that projectile points are found embedded in some carcasses, and that Africa, where large animals evolved alongside hominins, kept most of its fauna. The climate hypothesis points to the rapid habitat changes at the end of the last glaciation. A 2025 review found the literature still deeply divided, though the balance of recent work favours a substantial human role acting together with climate.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megafauna).

name: Upper Paleolithic cave art
summary: Painted cave sites at Chauvet, Lascaux, and Sulawesi display evidence of symbolic expression and artistic production.
body:
Painted and engraved images in caves and rock shelters are the most conspicuous surviving record of Upper Palaeolithic symbolic behaviour. The subjects are overwhelmingly large animals (bison, horses, aurochs, deer, lions, rhinoceroses, mammoths), together with hand stencils, dots and geometric signs. Human figures are rare, and landscapes absent.

The practice was not a European invention. The oldest known figurative painting is a scene of human-like figures and a pig from Leang Karampuang on Sulawesi, dated to about 51,200 years ago; a hand stencil on Muna, also in Indonesia, has been dated to around 67,800. In Europe the red discs and hand stencils of El Castillo in Spain are about 40,000 years old, the lions and rhinoceroses of Chauvet in France roughly 35,000, the horses of Lascaux about 17,000 and the bison of Altamira about 15,500.

The pigments are earth colours and charcoal (red and yellow ochre, haematite, manganese oxide), applied with finger, pad or brush, or blown around a hand to leave a stencil. Many images use the natural relief of the rock, and many are deep inside caves that had to be lit and worked in for long periods.

Why they were made is unknown. Hunting magic, shamanic practice, initiation, record-keeping and teaching have all been proposed, and none of them can be tested.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_painting).

name: Neanderthals disappear
summary: The last Neanderthal populations in Iberia and the Caucasus went extinct following millennia of overlap with modern humans.
body:
Part of [Out of Africa dispersal](event:out-of-africa). Neanderthals were a human species that occupied Europe and western and central Asia through the Middle and Late Pleistocene, from about 55 degrees north down to the Levant, and as far east as Denisova Cave in Siberia. They disappear around 40,000 years ago, though populations in southern Iberia and at Gibraltar may have persisted to 35,000 or 32,000.

They were stocky and powerfully built (males averaging about 1.65 metres and 75 kilograms), with a long low skull, a heavy continuous brow ridge and a projecting mid-face. Their brains were larger than the modern average, around 1,640 cubic centimetres in males, though organised somewhat differently.

They made Mousterian stone tools using prepared-core technique, maintained fire, hunted large game, ate a wide range of plants, used ochre and manganese pigments, and buried at least some of their dead. Claims that they made cave art rest on uranium-series dates from three Spanish caves that would predate the arrival of modern humans, and remain contested.

About 2 per cent of the genome of every living non-African is Neanderthal, and roughly a fifth of the Neanderthal genome survives, distributed in fragments across modern people. Their disappearance is generally attributed to some combination of competition with modern humans, chronically small and fragmented populations, and climate instability, rather than to any single cause.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neanderthal).

name: Last Glacial Maximum
summary: Ice sheets achieved their maximum extent and sea levels dropped approximately 125 metres below present values.
body:
Part of [Quaternary ice ages begin](event:quaternary-ice-ages). The Last Glacial Maximum was the most recent peak of the ice ages, between about 26,000 and 19,000 years ago. Around 21,000 years ago global mean temperature was roughly 6 °C below today's, and sea level stood about 125 metres lower.

The Laurentide ice sheet covered Canada and reached the Missouri and Ohio rivers, standing over three kilometres thick at its dome; the Fennoscandian sheet covered northern Europe with its margin running through Germany and Poland; Patagonia, the Alps, the Andes and the Himalaya carried ice of their own. Permanent ice covered about 8 per cent of the Earth's surface and a quarter of its land.

Water locked into that ice exposed continental shelf. Beringia joined Siberia to Alaska, Doggerland joined Britain to the continent, and Sundaland joined the Indonesian islands to mainland Asia. Those are the surfaces people walked across, and most of the archaeology of that walking is now under water.

The world was also drier and dustier than today. Deserts expanded, forest contracted into refugia, and steppe and tundra covered enormous areas. Human populations in Europe fell (by as much as 60 per cent on some estimates) and concentrated in southern refuges. The retreat of the ice from about 19,000 years ago opened the routes to [the Americas](event:americas-peopling).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Glacial_Maximum).

name: Peopling of the Americas
summary: Humans crossed Beringia and dispersed southward along the Pacific coast, colonizing two empty continents.
body:
Part of [Out of Africa dispersal](event:out-of-africa). The Americas were the last continents people reached. The academic consensus places arrival between about 20,000 and 15,000 years ago, by way of Beringia, the land bridge exposed between Siberia and Alaska while sea level was low.

Genetic work describes the sequence. An Ancient Beringian population separated from Siberians around 36,000 years ago, was effectively isolated by about 25,000, and split into the lineages ancestral to later Native American populations between 17,000 and 14,500 years ago.

The route south was long assumed to be the ice-free corridor between the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets, but that corridor became biologically passable only around 13,000 to 12,000 years ago, which is too late for the earliest sites. A Pacific coastal route, supported by kelp forests and marine resources, is now the more common explanation.

Monte Verde in southern Chile, at 14,500 years, was the first site widely accepted as older than the Clovis culture, and others followed: Buttermilk Creek in Texas at 15,500, Paisley Caves in Oregon at 14,300, Swan Point in Alaska at 14,000. Human footprints at White Sands in New Mexico have been dated to as much as 23,000 years ago; that dating has been challenged and re-defended and is not settled. However it began, the spread was fast, and people reached the southern end of South America within a few thousand years of entering the continent.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlement_of_the_Americas).

name: Domestication of the dog
summary: Wolves became the first domesticated animal, thousands of years before any crop or livestock.
body:
The dog was the first domesticated animal, and the only one domesticated by hunter-gatherers, thousands of years before any crop or any livestock. Its ancestor is the grey wolf, or rather an extinct wolf population from which modern wolves also descend.

Genetic divergence between the dog and wolf lineages is estimated at 40,000 to 20,000 years ago, which is an upper bound on domestication rather than a date for it. The oldest remains that are undisputedly dogs are more recent: the Erralla dog from northern Spain, 17,400 to 17,100 years old, and the Bonn-Oberkassel burial in Germany, about 14,200 years old, in which a dog was interred with two people, the earliest known joint burial of the two species, and evidence that the animal had been cared for through a serious illness.

Where it happened is unresolved. A 2021 review argued for Siberia around 23,000 years ago, with dogs spreading east into the Americas and west across Eurasia; western Europe and East Asia have also been proposed. Ancient genomes indicate at least two source populations: early dogs of north-eastern Europe, Siberia and the Americas share one origin, while those of the Middle East, Africa and southern Europe carry ancestry from another.

The domestication of [livestock and crops](event:animal-domestication) followed only after the end of the last glaciation.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origin_of_the_domestic_dog).

name: Younger Dryas cold snap
summary: The warming world returned to near-glacial conditions for over a millennium, then warmed again within decades.
body:
Part of [Quaternary ice ages begin](event:quaternary-ice-ages). The Younger Dryas was a return to near-glacial conditions between about 12,900 and 11,700 years ago, in the middle of the warming that followed the [Last Glacial Maximum](event:lgm). It is named after *Dryas octopetala*, an arctic flower whose pollen reappears in Scandinavian lake sediments from this interval.

The cooling was concentrated in the northern hemisphere: about 3 °C over North America, 2 to 6 °C in Europe and up to 10 °C in Greenland, where ice cores record the change taking three years or less. Winters were far colder while summers changed little. The southern hemisphere warmed at the same time, the seesaw pattern expected if the cause was a slowdown of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, which carries heat northward, and that is the consensus explanation.

What weakened the circulation is less certain. The traditional answer, a sudden discharge of meltwater from glacial Lake Agassiz into the North Atlantic, has little direct geological support; a Mackenzie River route has been proposed instead, and so has a cluster of volcanic eruptions immediately beforehand. A comet impact has been argued for repeatedly and is rejected by most specialists.

It ended as abruptly as it began, with warming of several degrees over about fifty years. That termination defines the start of the [Holocene](event:holocene), and the pressure the cold snap put on foragers in the Levant is often connected to the beginnings of [agriculture](event:agriculture).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Younger_Dryas).

name: Start of the Holocene
summary: The current interglacial commenced, establishing the stable, warm climate in which all human civilisation developed.
body:
The Holocene is the current geological epoch, beginning 11,700 years before 2000 and continuing to the present. It is the interglacial that followed the last glaciation, and every settled human society has existed within it.

Its base is defined not by a date but by a physical section: a horizon in the NGRIP2 ice core from central Greenland marking the end of the [Younger Dryas](event:younger-dryas), ratified as the epoch's global stratotype in 2008. The warming it records was several degrees within a few decades.

Three ages were formally defined in 2018. The Greenlandian runs from 11,700 to 8,200 years ago; the Northgrippian from 8,200 to 4,200, beginning at the 8.2-kiloyear cold event caused by the final drainage of the North American proglacial lakes; and the Meghalayan from 4,200 years ago to the present, beginning with a drought of roughly two centuries recorded across the northern hemisphere.

Sea level rose tens of metres over the first few thousand years as the ice sheets melted, then stabilised. The climate has been comparatively steady, though not without variability, including the 8.2-kiloyear event and cycles of between one and two and a half thousand years. [Agriculture](event:agriculture) was adopted independently in several regions between about 10,000 and 7,000 years ago.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocene).
